docs.title: Computer Vision Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most computer vision tutorials either stay at "here's a filter" forever, or jump straight to a pretrained model with no idea what it's actually doing underneath. This course builds the whole real stack: classical OpenCV operations run against real images, a real CNN trained from scratch and watched as it actually learns, real pretrained detectors and segmentation models run and evaluated locally, real optical flow and tracking on real video frames, real OCR against real text, and real vision transformer and embedding-based retrieval, all run locally — no cloud vision API, no account, no managed service standing in for understanding.

This course was written and run against a real local Python vision stack — OpenCV, scikit-image, PyTorch and torchvision — with every pixel, gradient, bounding box, mask and tracked point computed on this machine, not asserted from documentation. Where a real result was honest but unglamorous (a detector that missed, a tracker that drifted, a metric that didn't move), it's reported exactly as measured.

It assumes basic Python comfort and does not re-teach general machine learning fundamentals (training loops, loss functions, optimizers) — for that foundation, see the AI/ML Mastery Path. It also does not cover deploying vision models to microcontrollers or edge accelerators (TFLite Micro, NPUs, ESP32-CAM) — for that, see the Edge AI Mastery Path; this course stays at normal desktop/cloud-scale compute throughout.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Run it yourself. A real local Python environment with opencv-python, scikit-image, torch and torchvision is all this course's core lessons need — no account, no cloud bill, no managed vision API.
  • Read the "What was run" note at the top of each lesson. The overwhelming majority of this course's images, metrics, and detections come from real, observed runs against real pixels; anything that genuinely couldn't be run locally (massive-scale pretraining, specialized hardware) says so plainly.
  • Do the "predict, then run" exercises. Vision has several behaviors (what a filter kernel actually does to an edge, where IoU breaks down, how a tracker drifts) that are easy to miss from reading alone and genuinely clarifying to watch happen on a real image.
  • Do the projects. Each one is a real, runnable pipeline against real images or video, not a diagram.

docs.title: Level 1 · Image Fundamentals & Classical CV
docs.text:
Before any neural network, an image is just a grid of numbers — and most of what "computer vision" actually does is linear algebra and statistics applied to that grid. This level builds the classical toolkit directly on real images with OpenCV: reading and manipulating pixels, filtering and convolution, thresholding, contour and shape analysis, keypoint detection and matching, and the classical (pre-deep-learning) detection techniques that still matter for simple, constrained problems.

By the end of this level you can read, transform, filter, segment, and analyze a real image using nothing but classical image processing — and you'll have built a real, working document-scanner pipeline from scratch.

docs.title: Images as Arrays: Pixels, Channels & Color Spaces
What was run
docs.text: A real 512×512 color photograph (skimage.data.astronaut(), a real bundled sample image, not synthetic noise) inspected directly as a NumPy array — its shape, dtype, and individual pixel values — then run through a deliberately misapplied color-space conversion to measure, in real bytes, exactly what the classic "my colors are wrong" bug actually does to an image.

docs.title: A real image is just a 3D array of integers
docs.text:
img = data.astronaut()
print(f"shape={img.shape} dtype={img.dtype} min={img.min()} max={img.max()}")

REAL image: shape=(512, 512, 3) dtype=uint8 min=0 max=255
real pixel at row=100,col=100 (RGB order from skimage): [187 176 169]

A real 512×512 image with 3 channels is nothing more than 786,432 individual 8-bit integers (0–255), arranged as height × width × channels. img[100, 100] genuinely returns [187, 176, 169] — three real numbers, nothing more exotic.

docs.title: A real, measured channel-order bug
docs.text:
wrong = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)   # misapplied -- img is already RGB
mismatch = np.sum(wrong != correct)

real pixel at (100,100) if treated as already-correct RGB: [187 176 169]
real pixel at (100,100) after the WRONG conversion:        [169 176 187]
real byte-level mismatch: 456406/786432 bytes differ (58.0% of all pixel channel values)

A real, measured, exact number: misapplying a BGR↔RGB conversion to data that was already in the right order silently scrambled 58.0% of every channel value in the image — not a subtle tint shift, a genuine, massive corruption, visible the instant the image is displayed, yet the code runs without a single error or warning.

docs.title: A real, verified round trip
docs.text:
cv2.imwrite("astronaut_real.png", cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2BGR))
reloaded_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(cv2.imread("astronaut_real.png"), cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

real save-then-reload round trip (RGB -> BGR on disk -> back to RGB): pixel-exact match = True

Converted correctly both directions, the real saved-and-reloaded image is byte-for-byte identical to the original — confirming the conversion itself is lossless; only misapplying it (as the mismatch check above did deliberately) causes real damage.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every pixel in a color image is stored as 3 numbers, but libraries disagree on the real order those 3 numbers are stored in: scikit-image, matplotlib, and PIL/Pillow all use RGB (red first); OpenCV's cv2.imread() and cv2.imwrite() use BGR (blue first) for historical reasons. Neither order is wrong — they're just a real, fixed convention each library commits to — but mixing data from one convention into a function that expects the other, as this lesson's deliberate COLOR_BGR2RGB misapplication demonstrates, silently swaps the real red and blue channels for every single pixel, with no error to catch it.

The real 58.0% mismatch figure (not 100%) makes sense once you look at what the conversion actually does: it swaps channels 0 and 2 (red and blue) and leaves channel 1 (green) untouched — so only pixels where the real red and blue values actually differ from each other end up changed, which happens to be true for about 58% of this real photograph's pixels.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Loading an image with cv2.imread() and passing it straight into a function expecting RGB (most plotting, most pretrained deep learning models) without converting — this lesson's real 58.0% mismatch is exactly what that silent bug produces, with the error showing up as "the image looks wrong" rather than a program crash.
  • Assuming a color-space bug will be obvious — on an image with large uniform regions, this exact same bug can look subtle rather than dramatically wrong, which is often why it quietly ships.
  • Converting twice, or converting without knowing the real current order — this lesson's round-trip check confirms a correct double conversion is lossless, but Lesson 2 covers the simpler, real failure mode: forgetting whether you've converted at all.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Load skimage.data.coffee() (a different real bundled sample image) and repeat this lesson's exact mismatch measurement. Confirm whether the real percentage of mismatched bytes comes out close to this lesson's 58.0%, or genuinely different — and explain, from the image's own real color content, why.

docs.title: Image I/O, Resizing & Color Space Conversions
What was run
docs.text: The same real 512×512 image, downscaled to a quarter size and restored back to full size through three different real OpenCV interpolation methods, with the real quality loss of each measured by mean squared error (MSE) against the untouched original — plus a real aspect-ratio-distortion check and a real RGB↔HSV round trip.

docs.title: Real interpolation methods, measured, not assumed
docs.text:
small = cv2.resize(img, (w // 4, h // 4), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
for name, interp in methods.items():
    restored = cv2.resize(small, (w, h), interpolation=interp)
    mse = np.mean((img.astype(np.float64) - restored.astype(np.float64)) ** 2)

INTER_NEAREST : real MSE = 297.4800
INTER_LINEAR  : real MSE = 227.0267
INTER_CUBIC   : real MSE = 180.2516

A real, measured ranking: nearest-neighbor (just copying the closest pixel) produced the most real error, linear interpolation did meaningfully better, and cubic interpolation did best of the three — exactly the order each method's actual computation would predict, confirmed by measurement rather than taken on faith.

docs.title: A real, deliberate distortion
docs.text:
distorted = cv2.resize(img, (400, 100))  # ignores the real original aspect ratio

REAL distortion check: original aspect ratio=1.000, forced-resize aspect ratio=4.000

Resizing to an arbitrary fixed (width, height) genuinely stretched a square image into a real 4:1 rectangle — cv2.resize() has no concept of "preserve proportions" unless the caller computes the target size accordingly.

docs.title: A real, imperfect round trip
docs.text:
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
back = cv2.cvtColor(hsv, cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB)

REAL RGB->HSV->RGB round trip: max per-channel difference = 4, mean = 0.3455

A real, small, nonzero difference — HSV's conversion math involves division and real floating-point rounding that cv2's 8-bit integer pipeline cannot represent exactly, so a real round trip through HSV genuinely loses a few units of precision per pixel, even with no actual editing done in between.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Shrinking an image throws real information away — there are fewer pixels to represent the same picture — and every interpolation method guesses what the missing detail should have been. Nearest-neighbor guesses by literally copying the nearest known pixel, which is fast but creates real blocky artifacts; linear interpolation blends nearby pixels, smoothing those artifacts; cubic interpolation fits a smoother curve across a wider neighborhood, which is why this lesson's real MSE numbers came out lowest for cubic — it genuinely preserves more of the original signal when restoring a downscaled image, at the real cost of more computation per pixel.

Color space conversions are not always lossless round trips, even mathematically correct ones, because OpenCV's 8-bit pipeline keeps every intermediate value as an integer. HSV's hue/saturation math produces real fractional values that get rounded at every step, so a real RGB→HSV→RGB trip, as measured here, comes back close but not pixel-identical — a genuinely different outcome from Lesson 1's RGB↔BGR round trip, which is pixel-exact because it's just reordering integers, not computing new ones.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Resizing to a fixed (width, height) without preserving aspect ratio, as this lesson's deliberate 4:1 distortion shows — the usual real fix is computing the target size from a single scale factor, or padding to the target shape instead of stretching.
  • Assuming any color-space round trip is exact — this lesson's real mean=0.3455 difference after a single RGB→HSV→RGB trip means repeated real conversions (editing in HSV, converting back, re-converting later) can accumulate small but genuine, measurable drift.
  • Picking an interpolation method by habit (always INTER_LINEAR) rather than by what the resize is actually for — OpenCV's own documentation recommends INTER_AREA specifically for shrinking (used for the initial downscale in this lesson) and INTER_CUBIC or INTER_LINEAR for enlarging, which this lesson's real MSE numbers support for the upscale step.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Repeat this lesson's exact real MSE measurement, but downscale to 1/8 size instead of 1/4 before restoring, and confirm whether the real gap between INTER_NEAREST and INTER_CUBIC grows, shrinks, or stays proportionally similar as more real information is thrown away in the first place.

docs.title: Filtering & Convolution: Blur, Sharpen, Edge Detection
What was run
docs.text: A real, hand-written 2D convolution function, verified directly against OpenCV's own cv2.filter2D() on a real 20×20 image patch — which genuinely disagreed at first, for a real, specific reason investigated and resolved below — followed by real blur, sharpen, and edge-detection filters measured by their actual effect on image gradient strength.

docs.title: A real mismatch, investigated rather than ignored
docs.text:
manual_result = manual_convolve(small, box_kernel, pad_mode="reflect")
cv2_result_wrong_border = cv2.filter2D(small, -1, box_kernel, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT)

REAL manual convolution vs cv2.filter2D (mismatched border modes): max diff = 16.666667

A real, nonzero mismatch — not floating-point noise, a genuine disagreement of up to 16.67 intensity levels. Investigating directly: NumPy's "reflect" pad mode and OpenCV's BORDER_REFLECT are two different real reflection conventions — BORDER_REFLECT duplicates the edge pixel (cba|abc|cba), while NumPy's "reflect" (and OpenCV's own BORDER_REFLECT_101) does not (cb|abc|ba). Using the correctly matching pair:

cv2_result_correct = cv2.filter2D(small, -1, box_kernel, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)

REAL manual convolution vs cv2.filter2D (matching border modes):   max diff = 5.68e-14

A real difference of 5.68e-14 is floating-point noise, not a disagreement — the hand-written convolution is now confirmed, pixel-for-pixel, to compute exactly what OpenCV's own optimized implementation computes.

docs.title: Real filters, measured by their actual effect on image detail
docs.text:
def edge_energy(image):
    gx, gy = cv2.Sobel(image, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0), cv2.Sobel(image, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1)
    return np.mean(np.sqrt(gx ** 2 + gy ** 2))

original (no blur)  : 62.3135
box blur (9x9)       : 33.8058
gaussian blur (9x9)  : 41.2770

real sharpened edge energy: 113.4949 (vs original 62.3135)
real correlation between Sobel-magnitude and Laplacian edge maps: 0.6069

Both real blurs genuinely reduced measured edge energy (detail was lost), with box blur losing more than Gaussian blur; the real unsharp-mask sharpening nearly doubled edge energy, confirming it does the opposite. Sobel and Laplacian — two different real edge-detection formulas — only correlate at 0.6069, a real, measurable reminder that "edge detector" doesn't mean one single, interchangeable thing.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Convolution slides a small kernel of numbers across every position in an image and computes a weighted sum of the pixels underneath it; a blur kernel averages neighbors (smoothing detail), a sharpening kernel amplifies local differences (the unsharp mask here does this by adding back a scaled copy of the high-frequency detail a blur removed), and Sobel/Laplacian kernels specifically respond to local intensity changes — which is what makes them edge detectors. This lesson's real, hand-verified implementation proves that's genuinely all cv2.filter2D() is doing under the hood, no matter how different the result looks for each kernel.

The real border-mode mismatch this lesson hit and resolved is a direct, concrete illustration of why "verify, don't assume" matters even for something as basic as convolution: two libraries' default behavior at image edges can differ in a way that's completely invisible until you check pixel values directly, and the real consequence (up to 16.67 intensity levels off, concentrated exactly at the border) could easily be mistaken for a deeper bug in a less-isolated test.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming two libraries' "reflect" padding means the same thing — this lesson's own real investigation found NumPy's "reflect" matches OpenCV's BORDER_REFLECT_101 (OpenCV's actual default), not the similarly-named BORDER_REFLECT.
  • Treating Sobel and Laplacian as interchangeable "the edge detector" — this lesson's real 0.6069 correlation shows they genuinely disagree on a large fraction of the image; Sobel responds to directional gradients, Laplacian to the second derivative (curvature), and a real pipeline should pick based on which property actually matters for the task.
  • Sharpening by naively scaling up a Laplacian or Sobel result directly, rather than adding back high-frequency detail (the unsharp-mask approach this lesson used) — the naive version tends to amplify real sensor noise along with real edges, since both have high local gradient magnitude.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write your own hand-rolled Gaussian blur (generate a real 2D Gaussian kernel from its formula, then reuse this lesson's manual_convolve) and verify it against cv2.GaussianBlur() the same way this lesson verified its box filter — confirming the match (or finding, and investigating, a new real discrepancy of your own).

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real grayscale photograph of coins (skimage.data.coins()) converted to a binary foreground/background mask three different real ways — a fixed threshold, Otsu's automatically-computed threshold, and adaptive thresholding — then cleaned up with real morphological operations, including a direct, measured test of how many genuinely isolated noise pixels survive an opening operation.

docs.title: A real, data-computed threshold vs. a guessed one
docs.text:
_, global_thresh = cv2.threshold(img, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
otsu_value, otsu_thresh = cv2.threshold(img, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)

REAL Otsu-computed threshold value: 107.0
real foreground pixel count -- fixed threshold(127): 34469 (29.6%)
real foreground pixel count -- Otsu threshold(107.0): 45117 (38.8%)
real foreground pixel count -- adaptive threshold: 81257 (69.8%)

A real, meaningfully different outcome depending on method: the arbitrary fixed value of 127 missed real coin pixels that Otsu's threshold — computed directly from this image's own real pixel-intensity histogram, not guessed — correctly included. Adaptive thresholding, which computes a local rather than single global threshold, classified far more of the image as foreground, since it reacts to real local contrast rather than one fixed brightness cutoff.

docs.title: Real morphological operations, measured by real pixel counts
docs.text:
eroded = cv2.erode(otsu_thresh, kernel, iterations=1)
dilated = cv2.dilate(otsu_thresh, kernel, iterations=1)
opened = cv2.morphologyEx(otsu_thresh, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)

original (Otsu)      : 45117
erode (5x5, 1 iter)  : 27753 (shrinks real foreground)
dilate (5x5, 1 iter) : 57947 (grows real foreground)
open (erode->dilate) : 41309 (removes small real noise specks)
close (dilate->erode): 47731 (fills small real holes)

docs.title: A real, direct noise-removal test
docs.text:
added_mask = otsu_thresh[rows, cols] == 0  # count noise actually added to real background
noisy[rows, cols] = 255
opened_noisy = cv2.morphologyEx(noisy, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, kernel)
survived = (opened_noisy[rows[added_mask], cols[added_mask]] == 255).sum()

REAL noise-removal check: 128 isolated real noise pixels actually added to background,
3/128 survived after opening

A real, specific, checked-at-the-exact-pixel-level result: of 128 genuinely isolated single-pixel noise points added to the real image, opening removed 125 of them (97.7%) — the 3 that survived happened to land close enough to real existing coin foreground to be preserved rather than erased.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Otsu's method works by testing every possible threshold value and picking the one that best separates the image's real pixel-intensity histogram into two groups with minimum within-group variance — this lesson's real 107.0 is the specific value this particular image's histogram produced, not a constant that works for every image. Adaptive thresholding instead computes a separate local threshold for each neighborhood, which is why it classified so much more of this lesson's image as foreground: real uneven lighting across the photo means no single global cutoff, Otsu's included, can be correct everywhere at once.

Erosion and dilation both work by sliding a structuring element (this lesson's 5×5 square) across the image and requiring every pixel under it to be foreground (erosion) or at least one to be (dilation) — which is exactly why a single isolated noise pixel, with no foreground neighbors at all, cannot survive erosion: there is no position where a full 5×5 block of foreground exists around it. Opening is erosion followed by dilation, which is why this lesson's real, pixel-level test found 125 of 128 genuinely isolated noise points removed: they die in the erosion step and, having been full erased, have nothing left to dilate back.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Picking a single fixed threshold value by eye and assuming it generalizes — this lesson's real 127 missed over 9,000 real foreground pixels compared to Otsu's data-driven 107, on this one specific image alone.
  • Using global thresholding (fixed or Otsu) on an image with real uneven lighting — this lesson's real adaptive threshold classified 69.8% of the image as foreground versus Otsu's 38.8%, a difference entirely explained by real local contrast that a single global cutoff cannot represent.
  • Assuming opening always removes only noise — this lesson's real baseline comparison (45117 → 41309, even with zero added noise) shows opening also erodes small genuine structures (thin coin edges, in this case), not just synthetic salt-and-pepper speckles.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Repeat this lesson's real noise-removal test with a larger structuring element (9x9 instead of 5x5) and measure whether the real survival count drops further below 3/128, or whether it also starts eroding more of the genuine coin shapes — finding, by direct measurement, the real tradeoff point for this specific image.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Real contour detection run on the binary coin mask from Lesson 4, filtered first by area, then — after a real, investigated discovery that area filtering alone wasn't enough — by a real circularity measurement, to arrive at a genuinely correct count of real coin-shaped objects.

docs.title: Real contours, found and measured
docs.text:
contours, hierarchy = cv2.findContours(cleaned, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)

REAL contours found (raw): 33
real contour areas (pixels^2), sorted: [0, 0, 0, ..., 0, 1052, 1076, ..., 3026, 12353]

33 raw contours, most tiny (zero-area single-pixel noise) or real coin-sized — plus one real outlier at 12353 pixels², far larger than any other.

docs.title: A real filter that looked sufficient, until it wasn't
docs.text:
MIN_AREA = 500
real_coins = [c for c, a in zip(contours, areas) if a >= MIN_AREA]

real contours after filtering area >= 500: 22

22 contours survived — but checking each one's real circularity (4π·area / perimeter², where 1.0 is a perfect circle) found one, at area=12353.0, with circularity=0.0983: far too low to plausibly be a coin. Investigating directly with its real bounding box:

x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(c)
# area=12353.0 bbox=(0, 0, 329, 95), image shape=(303, 384)

A bounding box starting at the image's top-left corner, 329 pixels wide but only 95 tall — this is a real background/table-surface region that Otsu's threshold classified as foreground because of its brightness, not a coin at all. A pure area filter, with no shape check, let it straight through.

docs.title: The real, correct filter: area and circularity together
docs.text:
MIN_CIRCULARITY = 0.5
genuine_coins = [c for c, circ in zip(real_coins, circularities) if circ >= MIN_CIRCULARITY]

REAL second filter (circularity >= 0.5): 22 area-filtered contours -> 21 genuine coins

real mean circularity across 22 detected coins: 0.8283
real circularity range: [0.0983, 0.8962]
real circularity of a perfect 50x50 square (for comparison): 0.7854

21 real, genuinely coin-shaped contours, with the one background region correctly excluded — and a useful real reference point: a perfect square scores 0.7854, so most of these real coins (mean 0.8283, well above a square) are close to round, as expected, while the excluded background region's 0.0983 is nowhere close to either.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Contour area alone measures how big a shape is; it carries no information about what shape it is. This lesson's real background region happened to land in roughly the same area range as nothing in particular — it was simply large — and a filter that only checks "is this big enough to matter" has no way to distinguish a large, genuine coin from a large, irregular non-coin region. Circularity, computed from the real relationship between a shape's area and its perimeter, captures exactly the property area filtering misses: a circle packs the most area into the least perimeter of any shape, so anything with a long, thin, or irregular real outline — like this lesson's background region — scores far lower, regardless of its total size.

The real lesson here isn't "always filter by circularity" specifically — it's that any single real shape property, checked alone, can let through exactly the kind of object it wasn't designed to catch. Combining two different real, independent measurements (area and circularity) is what correctly separated this lesson's 21 genuine coins from both the tiny noise contours and the one large background region.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Filtering contours by area alone and assuming "big enough" means "the object I'm looking for" — this lesson's real background region at area 12353 would have passed any area threshold below that value, despite not being a coin at all.
  • Checking a derived shape metric like circularity without also sanity-checking it against a known reference — this lesson's real square comparison (0.7854) is what made it possible to say with confidence that 0.0983 is genuinely, not just numerically, non-circular.
  • Assuming RETR_EXTERNAL only returns "real objects" — it returns every real external contour the binary image actually contains, including large background regions that happened to threshold as foreground; the burden of distinguishing them is still on the caller's filtering logic.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Three real feature-detection algorithms — Harris corners, ORB, and SIFT — run against the same real image, then a direct, measured test of how well ORB's real keypoints survive a real 45-degree rotation versus a real 2× scale change, rather than assuming "ORB is rotation and scale invariant" from the textbook description alone.

docs.title: Three real detectors, three real outputs
docs.text:
harris = cv2.cornerHarris(img.astype(np.float32), blockSize=2, ksize=3, k=0.04)
kp_orb, des_orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=500).detectAndCompute(img, None)
kp_sift, des_sift = cv2.SIFT_create(nfeatures=500).detectAndCompute(img, None)

REAL Harris corners above threshold: 1708
REAL ORB keypoints detected: 500, descriptor shape: (500, 32) dtype=uint8
REAL SIFT keypoints detected: 500, descriptor shape: (500, 128) dtype=float32

Three real, genuinely different outputs: Harris finds 1,708 raw corner-like points with no descriptor at all (just locations); ORB produces a compact 32-byte binary descriptor per keypoint; SIFT produces a much larger 128-dimensional floating-point descriptor per keypoint — a real, measurable difference in both size and type that directly affects matching speed and memory later in this course.

docs.title: A real, measured rotation-invariance test
docs.text:
rotated = cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (w, h))  # the same real image, rotated 45 degrees
matches = bf.match(des_orb, des_orb_rot)
good_matches = [m for m in matches if m.distance < 40]

REAL ORB keypoints on the same image rotated 45 degrees: 500
real ORB matches between original and rotated image: 332 total, 298 with distance < 40

A real 89.8% good-match rate (298 of 332) — ORB's descriptors for the same physical points genuinely remained close enough in Hamming distance to be correctly matched after a real 45-degree rotation.

docs.title: The same real test, applied to scale instead of rotation
docs.text:
half = cv2.resize(img, (w // 2, h // 2))  # the same real image, at half the original scale

REAL ORB keypoints on the same image at half scale: 445
real ORB matches between original and half-scale image: 191 total, 141 with distance < 40

A real, meaningfully lower 73.8% good-match rate (141 of 191) — the exact same algorithm, on the exact same image, handled a real scale change measurably worse than it handled a real rotation.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
ORB computes an orientation for each keypoint and rotates its sampling pattern to match, which is specifically why this lesson's real rotation test held up well: the descriptor is explicitly built to compensate for rotation. Scale is handled differently — ORB detects keypoints across a real but limited multi-scale pyramid, and a keypoint's descriptor is computed at roughly the scale it was detected at, not re-normalized the way SIFT does with its own, more expensive scale-space search. This lesson's real, lower match rate under scaling is a direct, measured consequence of that real design tradeoff, not a flaw in the test.

The real reason this course measures this rather than stating it is that "invariant to rotation and scale" is often repeated as a blanket description of these algorithms without the real, honest caveat that how much invariance a specific algorithm delivers is itself a real, measurable, and uneven quantity — exactly what this lesson's two different real percentages (89.8% vs. 73.8%) demonstrate directly.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "scale and rotation invariant" as an absolute guarantee rather than a real, measurable degree of robustness — this lesson's own numbers show the same algorithm handling two different transformations with a real 16-point-percentage gap.
  • Choosing ORB over SIFT (or vice versa) based on reputation alone rather than this lesson's real, concrete differences: ORB's binary descriptor is dramatically cheaper to store and match (32 bytes vs. SIFT's 512 bytes per keypoint, both real, measured sizes), which matters when matching is run at scale in Level 3's detection work.
  • Running a matcher like BFMatcher with the wrong distance metric for the descriptor type — this lesson used NORM_HAMMING specifically because ORB's descriptor is binary; SIFT's floating-point descriptor needs NORM_L2 instead, and mismatching the two produces meaningless real distance values.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, known perspective warp applied to a real image — a ground-truth transformation this script knows exactly — then genuinely forgotten: ORB keypoints detected on both images independently, matched, and fed into cv2.findHomography() with RANSAC to see how closely the algorithm can recover a transformation it was never told, measured against the real ground truth it actually used.

docs.title: A real, known warp, recovered from real matched keypoints alone
docs.text:
true_H = np.array([[1.05, 0.08, 20], [0.03, 0.98, -15], [0.0002, 0.0001, 1.0]])
warped = cv2.warpPerspective(img, true_H, (w, h))
...
est_H, mask = cv2.findHomography(src_pts, dst_pts, cv2.RANSAC, 5.0)

real raw matches found: 548
real RANSAC inliers: 532/548 (97.1%)

A real 97.1% inlier rate — RANSAC correctly identified 532 of 548 real matched keypoint pairs as consistent with a single real geometric transformation, discarding the rest as real mismatches.

docs.title: The real recovered transformation, checked against the real ground truth
docs.text:
elementwise_diff = np.abs(true_H / true_H[2, 2] - est_H / est_H[2, 2])

real max element-wise difference: 0.672599

The raw matrix elements differ by up to 0.67 — but a homography matrix's raw numbers are not directly comparable the way a prediction and a label are; what actually matters is where real points end up after the transformation, checked next.

docs.title: The real, meaningful check: reprojection error at real points
docs.text:
true_projected = cv2.perspectiveTransform(test_points, true_H)
est_projected = cv2.perspectiveTransform(test_points, est_H)
errors = np.linalg.norm((true_projected - est_projected).reshape(-1, 2), axis=1)

REAL reprojection error at 5 real test points (pixels): [0.467 0.232 0.119 0.287 0.103]
real mean reprojection error: 0.2415 pixels

A real, sub-pixel mean error of 0.2415 pixels across five independently chosen test points — the estimated homography, built from nothing but matched ORB keypoints and RANSAC, places real points within a quarter of a pixel of where the true (and, to the estimation process, completely unknown) transformation actually sends them.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A homography matrix has 8 real degrees of freedom (9 numbers, one redundant scale factor), and in principle 4 correctly matched point pairs are enough to solve for it exactly. This lesson's real 532 inlier matches are drastically more than that minimum — which is precisely why RANSAC and the least-squares fit underlying cv2.findHomography() can average out the real, inevitable noise in individual keypoint positions and land this close to the true transformation, rather than being thrown off by any single bad match.

The reason raw matrix-element differences (this lesson's real 0.67 max) look large while the real, practically-meaningful reprojection error (0.24 pixels) is tiny comes down to how a homography's bottom row works: the small perspective terms (0.0002, 0.0001) interact multiplicatively with pixel coordinates in the hundreds, so a tiny real error there can look large in isolation while barely moving where an actual point lands — which is exactly why this lesson checks the real, geometrically meaningful quantity (where do points actually go) rather than stopping at the raw numbers.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing two homography matrices element-by-element and concluding "very different" without checking real reprojection error — this lesson's own numbers show a 0.67 raw difference corresponding to a genuinely tiny 0.24-pixel real-world effect.
  • Skipping RANSAC and fitting a homography to every real raw match directly — with 548 raw matches and at least some genuine mismatches among them, a direct least-squares fit with no outlier rejection would be pulled measurably off by the real bad matches RANSAC's own inlier/outlier split (532 vs. 16) explicitly identified and discarded.
  • Forgetting that a homography assumes a planar scene or pure camera rotation — this lesson's test image is effectively planar (a single 2D photograph), which is exactly the condition under which this kind of real recovery works this well; a genuinely 3D scene with real parallax would break this assumption.

docs.title: Exercise

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real battery of common training-time image augmentations — flip, rotation, brightness jitter, Gaussian noise, random crop, and cutout — each measured against the untouched original using structural similarity (SSIM), a real, standard image-similarity metric, to see what each augmentation actually does to an image quantitatively rather than just visually.

docs.title: Real SSIM measurements across every augmentation
docs.text:
flipped = cv2.flip(img, 1)
print(real_ssim(img, flipped))

horizontal flip          : SSIM=0.1456
rotate  5 degrees         : SSIM=0.3453
rotate 15 degrees         : SSIM=0.2259
rotate 45 degrees         : SSIM=0.1779
brightness +10            : SSIM=0.8820
brightness +40            : SSIM=0.8030
brightness +80            : SSIM=0.6886
gaussian noise sigma=5    : SSIM=0.8502
gaussian noise sigma=20   : SSIM=0.4215
gaussian noise sigma=50   : SSIM=0.1956
random crop + resize      : SSIM=0.2620
cutout (100x100 region)   : SSIM=0.9647 (real 10000 of 262144 pixels zeroed = 3.81%)

docs.title: A real, counter-intuitive finding worth taking seriously
docs.text: A horizontal flip — an augmentation that preserves every single real pixel value and the complete content of the image, just mirrored — scored a real 0.1456: SSIM's most dissimilar result of this entire lesson. A 100×100 cutout, which genuinely destroys 3.81% of the real image by zeroing it out entirely, scored 0.9647: SSIM's most similar result, after brightness and noise. By SSIM's own measurement, a flip "changes" the image far more than erasing a real patch of it does — which is backwards from what anyone looking at both images would say.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
SSIM compares small local windows at matching pixel coordinates between two images — it measures whether the patch at position (x, y) in image A looks like the patch at that same position (x, y) in image B. A flip moves nearly every piece of real content to a different coordinate, so almost none of those paired windows contain the same real content anymore, even though the image itself is fully intact and just mirrored. A cutout, by contrast, leaves 96.19% of the image's real pixels in their exact original positions, so the overwhelming majority of SSIM's compared windows still match closely — even though a real, coherent chunk of content is now simply gone.

The real lesson is specific and important for this course: SSIM (and position-based pixel metrics generally) measure spatial similarity, not semantic or content similarity. A flip is semantically almost identical to the original (same objects, same recognizability, mirrored) but spatially very different; a cutout is spatially almost identical (nearly every pixel in its original place) but has genuinely removed real information. Choosing an augmentation — or evaluating one — based on SSIM alone would get exactly these two cases backwards.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using SSIM (or any purely spatial pixel metric) to judge whether an augmentation is "too aggressive" for training — this lesson's real numbers show it can rate a content-preserving flip as more extreme than an actual information-destroying cutout.
  • Assuming an augmentation that looks subtle to a human (cutout, at only 3.81% of pixels) is therefore "safe" for training — the real information removed by a cutout can still matter enormously to a model if it happens to land on the one discriminative feature that mattered, regardless of what any pixel-similarity metric says.
  • Picking a single similarity metric and trusting it as a universal measure of "how much has this image changed" — this lesson's real, directly-contradictory flip-vs-cutout result is exactly why a metric needs to be chosen for what it actually measures, not applied as if "similarity" means one single thing.

docs.title: Exercise

Confirm the real SSIM this time comes back close to 1.0 — proving directly that the low 0.1456 score in this lesson came from spatial misalignment, not from any genuine difference in the image's real content.

docs.title: Classical Object Detection: Template Matching & Haar Cascades
What was run
docs.text: An honest, current discovery first: checking whether this course's real OpenCV install (version 5.0.0, newly released) still exposes Haar cascade face detection — it does not, which is itself worth documenting plainly. Then real template matching, run against a known real image patch, and deliberately pushed past its limits with real scale and rotation changes to find out exactly where, and how dangerously, it breaks.

docs.title: A real, honest finding: Haar cascades are gone from this OpenCV version
docs.text:
has_cascade_classifier = hasattr(cv2, "CascadeClassifier")
cascade_dir_contents = os.listdir(cv2.data.haarcascades)

REAL check: cv2.CascadeClassifier available in this OpenCV 5.0.0 install: False
real contents of cv2.data.haarcascades directory: ['__init__.py', '__pycache__']

A real, verified absence, not an assumption: OpenCV 5.0's Python bindings genuinely no longer expose cv2.CascadeClassifier, and the package ships zero .xml cascade files at all. Haar cascades — OpenCV's original, classical face/object detector, trained on simple intensity-difference features — have been superseded by DNN-based detectors like cv2.FaceDetectorYN (which this install does have, confirmed via hasattr), reflecting a real, current shift away from the classical technique this lesson was originally built around.

docs.title: Real template matching: a perfect, exact match
docs.text:
template = img[150:220, 230:300].copy()  # a real 70x70 patch cut from the image
result = cv2.matchTemplate(img, template, cv2.TM_CCOEFF_NORMED)

REAL template matching: true location=(230,150), found location=(230, 150), match confidence=1.000000

Matching a template against the exact same image it was cut from finds it perfectly — unsurprising, but a necessary real baseline before stress-testing the technique.

docs.title: Real scale robustness: confidence drops, but gracefully
docs.text:
scale=1.0 : found=(230, 150), expected~=(230, 150), confidence=1.0000
scale=0.9 : found=(204, 132), expected~=(207, 135), confidence=0.9842
scale=0.75: found=(166, 106), expected~=(172, 112), confidence=0.9417
scale=0.5 : found=(95, 56),  expected~=(115, 75),  confidence=0.8396

A real, honest, gradual decline — both confidence and positional accuracy degrade smoothly as scale changes, exactly as expected for a method with no built-in scale invariance.

docs.title: Real rotation robustness: a dangerous, high-confidence false positive
docs.text:
rotation= 0 deg: found=(230, 150), confidence=1.0000
rotation= 5 deg: found=(226, 150), confidence=0.9663
rotation=15 deg: found=(223, 153), confidence=0.9094
rotation=30 deg: found=(28, 235), confidence=0.9062

The real, important finding: at 15 degrees, template matching is still roughly in the right place. At 30 degrees, the reported confidence (0.9062) is barely lower than at 15 degrees — but the real found location (28, 235) is nowhere near the true rotated position. This is not a graceful degradation; it's a real, silent failure that looks just as confident as a correct match.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Template matching works by sliding the template over every real position in the image and computing how well pixel values correlate at each position — it has no concept of "this template, slightly rotated" unless the rotated version happens to correlate well somewhere else by coincidence, which is exactly what happened at 30 degrees: some other, unrelated region of the image apparently correlates with the un-rotated template nearly as well as the true, rotated target region does, once the true target's own pixels have been scrambled enough by rotation to no longer match well. The algorithm has no way to know this — it just reports wherever the real correlation score was highest, confident or not.

This is a direct, concrete illustration of why Haar cascades, and later CNN-based detectors (Level 3), exist: they're built with real invariance to pose and appearance variation baked into their design or training, specifically to avoid this lesson's real failure mode — a technique that looks confident right up until it's confidently wrong.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting a template-matching confidence score as a reliability signal on its own — this lesson's real 0.9062 at completely the wrong location proves the score alone cannot distinguish "correct match" from "coincidentally correlated elsewhere."
  • Assuming a classical technique's limitations degrade gracefully by default — this lesson's real scale test did degrade smoothly, but the real rotation test did not, and there was no way to know which one a given technique would do without actually testing both.
  • Assuming a cascade-based or any specific classical API will always be available in a given OpenCV install — this lesson's real, direct check caught a genuine, version-specific removal before it could silently break a downstream lesson or project.

docs.title: Exercise

Find the specific real rotation angle where the two curves actually diverge — where confidence stays high but the real found location has already gone wrong.

docs.title: Project: a Real Classical CV Pipeline (Document Scanner)
What was run
docs.text: Honest note: no real camera or photographed document is available in this environment, so this project builds a real, synthetic scene — a real white page with real printed-line patterns, placed at a real, known perspective angle against a real noisy background — and runs the exact, unmodified document-scanner pipeline against it that would run on an actual photo. Every step (edge detection, contour finding, corner ordering, perspective correction, thresholding) is real; only the input photo is synthetic, and that's stated plainly rather than presented as a real photograph.

docs.title: The real, complete pipeline, chained together
docs.text:
gray = cv2.cvtColor(scene, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
edges = cv2.Canny(cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0), 50, 150)
contours, _ = cv2.findContours(edges, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
for c in sorted(contours, key=cv2.contourArea, reverse=True)[:10]:
    approx = cv2.approxPolyDP(c, 0.02 * cv2.arcLength(c, True), True)
    if len(approx) == 4:
        page_contour = approx
        break

REAL pipeline found a 4-point contour: True

The real pipeline — edge detection, contour finding, and a 4-point polygon approximation — correctly isolated the page's outline from the real cluttered, noisy background with no manual intervention.

docs.title: Real corner accuracy, measured against the real ground truth
docs.text:
corner_errors = np.linalg.norm(ordered_found - ordered_true, axis=1)

REAL per-corner detection error (pixels): [1.4142135 1. 1. 1.]
real mean corner detection error: 1.10 pixels

A real, sub-2-pixel detection error at every one of the four corners — remarkably close, achieved entirely from edge and contour geometry, with no knowledge of where the page "should" be.

docs.title: A real, verified perspective correction
docs.text:
unwarp_H = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(ordered_found, dst_rect)
scanned = cv2.warpPerspective(scene, unwarp_H, (PAGE_W, PAGE_H))

real rows containing a detected horizontal text line after unwarping: 51

Using the detected corners (not the ground truth) to compute the unwarping transform, the real recovered page has exactly the true aspect ratio, and the real printed lines — skewed and foreshortened in the original scene — show up as genuinely straight, horizontal rows of dark pixels after correction, exactly as a properly flattened scan should look.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project is every technique from this level, chained into one real pipeline, each stage's output feeding the next: Lesson 3's blur and edge detection isolate real boundaries; Lesson 5's contour finding and polygon approximation turn those boundaries into a candidate 4-cornered shape; Lesson 7's perspective-transform math straightens it back into a flat rectangle. The real 1.10-pixel corner accuracy this project achieved is a direct consequence of Lesson 5's lesson about combining filters (here, picking the largest-area, exactly-4-point contour) rather than trusting any single raw signal.

The real reason this pipeline works from the detected corners rather than ground truth, as this project specifically verified, is that's exactly the real-world condition a document scanner actually operates under — it never knows where the page corners truly are, only what the image itself reveals through real edges and contours.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Skipping real corner ordering before computing the perspective transform — cv2.findContours() returns points in an arbitrary real order, and feeding them into getPerspectiveTransform() out of order (not top-left/top-right/bottom-right/bottom-left) produces a real, badly distorted result even with perfectly accurate corner locations.
  • Assuming the largest contour is always the page — this project checked the largest 10 real contours for the first one that approximates to exactly 4 points, rather than trusting area alone, since a real cluttered background can produce a larger irrelevant contour.
  • Validating a scanner pipeline only by eye rather than against a real, independent check — this project's real aspect-ratio and corner-error measurements are what actually confirm correctness; a visually "pretty straight" result could still be subtly wrong in ways a quick look wouldn't catch.

Find the real blur strength at which the pipeline's 4-point contour detection starts failing to find the page at all, rather than just losing some precision.

docs.title: Level 2 · CNNs & Image Classification
docs.text:
Classical filters are hand-designed; a convolutional neural network learns its own filters directly from real data. This level builds that understanding from the ground up: why convolution and pooling make sense for images, a real CNN trained from scratch and watched as it actually learns, real pretrained architectures (ResNet) used as backbones, real transfer learning and fine-tuning, and the evaluation and visualization tools that reveal what a trained model actually picked up on — not just its final accuracy number.

By the end of this level you'll have trained, evaluated, and fine-tuned real image classifiers, and built a complete, real image classification project end to end.

docs.title: Why CNNs: Convolution, Pooling & Receptive Fields
What was run
docs.text: A real PyTorch nn.Conv2d layer, with its weights manually set to the exact same Sobel-X kernel from Level 1, run against the same real image and compared directly to cv2.Sobel() — plus real, measured checks of output-size formulas, shift-invariance under pooling, and receptive-field growth across stacked layers.

docs.title: A real CNN layer computing exactly the same thing as a classical filter
docs.text:
conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=1, kernel_size=3, padding=1, bias=False)
conv.weight[:] = torch.from_numpy(sobel_x_kernel).view(1, 1, 3, 3)

REAL CNN conv layer (manually set to Sobel-X weights) vs cv2.Sobel (full image): max diff=923.000000
REAL same comparison, interior pixels only (excluding the 1px border): max diff=0.000000

A real, exact match at every interior pixel (0.000000) — once the comparison excludes the image border. The real 923.0 discrepancy on the full image is, investigated directly, the exact same kind of real border-padding mismatch Level 1, Lesson 3 already found: PyTorch's padding=1 pads with zeros, while cv2.Sobel() reflects at the border — two real, different conventions, not a math error. Interior pixels, unaffected by either convention, prove the two are computing the identical real operation.

docs.title: Real pooling and real receptive-field growth, both measured directly
docs.text:
no_pool_diff = torch.mean(torch.abs(img_t - shifted_t)).item()
pool_diff = torch.mean(torch.abs(pool(img_t) - pool(shifted_t))).item()

mean abs difference WITHOUT pooling: 7.0621
mean abs difference WITH 2x2 max pooling: 5.7749

center.backward()

2 stacked 3x3 conv layers: real measured receptive field area = 25 pixels (expected 5x5=25)
3 stacked 3x3 conv layers: real measured receptive field area = 49 pixels (expected 7x7=49)
5 stacked 3x3 conv layers: real measured receptive field area = 121 pixels (expected 11x11=121)

A real, measurable reduction in sensitivity to a 1-pixel shift after pooling (5.7749 vs 7.0621), and real, exact receptive-field areas — measured directly via gradient flow, not just computed from a formula — confirming each stacked 3×3 layer genuinely grows the region of input that can influence one output unit by exactly 2 pixels per side.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A convolutional layer is not a different kind of operation from the classical filters in Level 1 — it's the exact same sliding-window weighted sum, with the one real difference that a CNN's weights are learned rather than hand-designed, as this lesson's manually-set Sobel weights prove directly by matching cv2.Sobel() pixel-for-pixel. Pooling reduces spatial resolution and, as this lesson measured, reduces sensitivity to small real translations — not eliminating it, but genuinely dampening it, which is exactly the kind of approximate shift-tolerance a classifier benefits from. Stacking layers grows the receptive field — how much of the real input ultimately influences one output value — linearly with each additional 3×3 layer, confirmed here by directly measuring gradient flow rather than trusting the formula alone.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a CNN's internal filters as mysterious or fundamentally different from classical image filters — this lesson's real, exact interior-pixel match (manually set Sobel weights) proves a single conv layer is a classical filter; what's different is that, during training, the network discovers its own useful kernels instead of a human hand-designing them.
  • Assuming max pooling makes a network fully shift-invariant — this lesson's real numbers show pooling reduces, but does not eliminate, sensitivity to a 1-pixel shift (5.7749, not 0).
  • Comparing two convolution implementations on a full image without checking border-pixel handling separately — this lesson's real investigation (same discipline as Level 1, Lesson 3) is what correctly distinguished a real border-convention difference from an actual computation error.

docs.title: Building a CNN From Scratch in PyTorch
What was run
docs.text: A real, small CNN (SimpleCNN: two conv layers, two pooling layers, two fully-connected layers) built from scratch in PyTorch, run with a real random input batch to confirm shapes, with every real parameter counted layer by layer, and a real apples-to-apples comparison against an equivalent fully-connected layer to measure exactly how much weight sharing actually saves.

docs.title: A real forward pass, and every real parameter counted
docs.text:
model = SimpleCNN()
output = model(torch.randn(4, 3, 32, 32))

REAL forward pass: input shape=(4, 3, 32, 32), output shape=(4, 10)
real total trainable parameters in this CNN: 268,650
  conv1.weight        :      432 real parameters
  conv2.weight        :    4,608 real parameters
  fc1.weight          :  262,144 real parameters
  fc2.weight          :    1,280 real parameters

A real, honest, slightly surprising finding: this CNN's total parameter count (268,650) is actually higher than a naive single fully-connected layer mapping the same input straight to 10 classes (30,730) — because this specific small network's flatten-then-FC head (fc1's 262,144 parameters) dominates the total, not the convolutional layers.

docs.title: The real, fair comparison — and why it matters
docs.text:
fc_equivalent_params = (3 * 32 * 32) * (16 * 32 * 32) + (16 * 32 * 32)

REAL apples-to-apples comparison (same input -> same output shape):
  conv1 (shared 3x3 kernel, all positions): 448 real parameters
  equivalent fully-connected layer:          50,348,032 real parameters
  real ratio: 112,384x more parameters for the FC version

The real, meaningful comparison isn't "whole CNN vs. a single classification layer" — it's "what would it cost a fully-connected layer to produce the exact same output shape conv1 produces." Answered directly: a real, 112,384× more parameters. Weight sharing is real and dramatic — it just doesn't show up when comparing a whole small network's total parameter count against a single layer that skips straight to 10 output classes.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A convolutional layer reuses the exact same small set of weights (this lesson's 3×3×3 kernel, 448 numbers including bias) at every one of the 1,024 spatial positions in a 32×32 output — it never needs a separate weight for each position the way a fully-connected layer does. That's the real, structural source of the 112,384× gap this lesson measured directly: the FC equivalent needs a distinct weight for every (input-pixel, output-position) pair, while the conv layer needs only one small kernel, reused everywhere.

The real reason this lesson's overall network ended up larger than the naive single-layer comparison is that fc1 — the layer that flattens the convolutional output and maps it to a hidden layer — reintroduces exactly the problem convolution solves, at the boundary between the convolutional and fully-connected parts of the network. This is a real, genuine architectural tension that modern networks (Lesson 5's real ResNet backbone, among others) address with global pooling instead of a large flatten step, specifically to avoid this lesson's own fc1 from dominating the parameter count.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Repeating "CNNs have fewer parameters than fully-connected networks" as an unconditional fact — this lesson's own real total parameter count is a direct counterexample for this specific small architecture; the real savings are specifically in the convolutional layers, not guaranteed for the network as a whole.
  • Comparing a full CNN's parameter count to a single FC layer that skips straight to the final output, instead of to an FC layer that could produce the same intermediate output shape — this lesson's real 112,384x figure only appears once the comparison is made fair.
  • Not verifying that gradients actually reach every real layer after backward() — this lesson's final check confirmed every parameter, from conv1 through fc2, genuinely received a nonzero gradient, catching the class of real bug where a layer is accidentally detached from the computation graph.

docs.text: Replace this lesson's fc1 (which flattens all 32×8×8=2048 values) with nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1) followed by a much smaller linear layer (32 -> 128), and recompute the real total parameter count. Confirm by how much the real number drops, and connect that real reduction to what Lesson 5's real ResNet backbone actually does differently from this lesson's simple architecture.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text:
A real CNN, trained completely from scratch (random initial weights, no pretraining) for 5 real epochs on FashionMNIST — 60,000 real grayscale photographs of clothing items across 10 categories — with real loss and accuracy tracked every epoch, and a real, final test-set evaluation on 10,000 images the model never saw during training.

Honest note on dataset choice: this lesson originally targeted CIFAR-10, but its real download mirror was measured at under 2% progress after several real minutes — genuinely too slow for this environment. FashionMNIST, hosted on a different, fast real source (14 seconds for the full 60,000-image set), was used instead. It's grayscale rather than color, but every image is a real photograph of a real clothing item, not synthetic data.

docs.text:

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):

A real, steadily decreasing loss and steadily increasing accuracy — the exact shape a genuinely learning model should produce, run on this machine's real Apple GPU (mps) backend, not simulated or typed from memory.

docs.title: A real, honest test on unseen data
docs.text:
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    for images, labels in test_loader:
        ...

REAL final test accuracy (never seen during training): 0.8972

A real 89.72% on 10,000 completely held-out images — close to, but genuinely below, the final training accuracy of 90.46%, exactly the small, expected real gap between performance on data the model trained on versus data it didn't.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each real epoch processes all 60,000 training images once, in real random mini-batches of 128, computing a real gradient from each batch's loss and nudging every one of the model's weights slightly to reduce it. The real, steadily improving numbers across 5 epochs are direct evidence this is actually happening — a model with a bug in its training loop (gradients not flowing, a frozen layer) would show flat or erratic numbers instead, not this lesson's clean, monotonic improvement.

The real, small gap between training accuracy (90.46%) and test accuracy (89.72%) is the most basic real signal of whether a model has started overfitting — memorizing training-specific detail rather than learning generalizable patterns. A gap this small, after only 5 real epochs, suggests this particular model and dataset combination isn't yet overfitting meaningfully; Lesson 4 examines what happens to that real gap as training continues further.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reporting only training accuracy and treating it as the model's real performance — this lesson's real 90.46% training number alone would overstate how well the model actually generalizes; the real test figure (89.72%) is the honest number.
  • Assuming a slow download means a dataset or tool is broken, rather than investigating further — this lesson's own real experience (CIFAR-10's mirror measured, timed, and found genuinely too slow, then substituted honestly rather than silently claimed to have worked) is exactly the "verify, don't assume" discipline this course has used throughout.
  • Forgetting model.eval() before real evaluation — layers like dropout and batch normalization (used in later lessons) behave differently during training vs. evaluation, and skipping this switch silently produces real, incorrect evaluation numbers even though no error occurs.

docs.title: Data Augmentation & Regularization for Vision Models
What was run
docs.text: Two real, identically-seeded CNNs, trained for 15 real epochs each on FashionMNIST: one plain, one with real augmentation (random flips and rotations) and real dropout (0.4) — with the real train/test accuracy gap tracked every single epoch for both, to see not just whether regularization "works," but what it actually trades off.

docs.title: A real, growing overfitting gap, without regularization
docs.text:
plain_model = FashionCNN(dropout_p=0.0)

epoch  1/15: train=0.7863 test=0.8302 real train-test gap=-0.0439
epoch  5/15: train=0.9078 test=0.8977 real train-test gap=0.0101
epoch 10/15: train=0.9322 test=0.9119 real train-test gap=0.0203
epoch 15/15: train=0.9503 test=0.9192 real train-test gap=0.0311

A real, textbook overfitting signature: the gap starts negative (the model is still underfit early on) and climbs steadily positive as training continues, ending at a real +0.0311 — training accuracy pulling ahead of test accuracy, the model increasingly memorizing training-specific detail.

docs.title: A real, qualitatively different pattern with augmentation + dropout
docs.text:
reg_model = FashionCNN(dropout_p=0.4)  # trained on real flip+rotation augmented data

epoch  1/15: train=0.7151 test=0.8249 real train-test gap=-0.1098
epoch  5/15: train=0.8631 test=0.8816 real train-test gap=-0.0185
epoch 10/15: train=0.8831 test=0.8991 real train-test gap=-0.0160
epoch 15/15: train=0.8958 test=0.9034 real train-test gap=-0.0076

A real, completely different shape: the gap stays negative for all 15 epochs — test accuracy consistently higher than train accuracy, the opposite of the plain model's pattern.

docs.title: The real, honest complication
docs.text:
plain:          train=0.9503 test=0.9192 gap=0.0311
augmented+drop: train=0.8958 test=0.9034 gap=-0.0076

Regularization did exactly what it's supposed to do to the gap — but the real, final test accuracy tells a more complicated story: the plain model's real 0.9192 is actually higher than the regularized model's 0.9034. Reducing overfitting did not, in this specific real run, translate into a better real test result.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The regularized model's negative gap isn't actually a sign it's "better" at generalizing by some abstract measure — it's a real, direct, measurable consequence of dropout's mechanics: during training, dropout randomly disables 40% of the real units in that layer, artificially capping the model's measured training accuracy at a point the same network, with dropout disabled during evaluation, can beat. That's precisely why model.eval() (which turns dropout off) consistently reports a higher real number than model.train()'s reported accuracy throughout this run.

The real, more important finding is that the regularized model's final test accuracy (0.9034) didn't beat the plain model's (0.9192) despite a much cleaner train/test gap. This is a genuine, real instance of the bias-variance tradeoff: this particular combination of augmentation strength and dropout rate reduced the model's capacity to fit anything, including real, genuinely useful patterns, not just training-set noise — and on a dataset of 60,000 real images that wasn't yet overfitting badly in the first place (the plain model's own gap, 0.0311, is modest), that tradeoff didn't pay for itself within 15 real epochs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a shrinking (or negative) train/test gap as automatic proof that regularization "worked" — this lesson's own real numbers show the regularized model achieved a cleaner gap while still losing on raw real test accuracy.
  • Applying strong regularization (augmentation + dropout together) without first checking whether the real, unregularized model is actually overfitting badly enough to need it — this lesson's plain model's real gap of 0.0311 after 15 epochs is a comparatively mild overfit; a model badly overfitting (a real gap of 0.15 or more) would likely show regularization paying off much more clearly.
  • Forgetting that dropout changes measured training accuracy's meaning, not just its value — comparing a dropout model's real training accuracy directly to a non-dropout model's, as a measure of "how well is it learning," is comparing two numbers computed under genuinely different conditions.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real comparison with a much weaker real regularization setting (dropout_p=0.1, no augmentation) and check whether the real final test accuracy this time beats the plain model's 0.9192 — to find, empirically, whether a lighter real regularization touch helps where this lesson's stronger one did not.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real, pretrained ImageNet architectures — ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 — compared by real parameter count, then both run on the exact same real photograph (the astronaut image used throughout this course) to see not just whether they agree, but what they each actually predict, reported honestly even though neither gets it right.

docs.title: Real parameter counts, measured directly
docs.text:
params18 = sum(p.numel() for p in resnet18.parameters())
params50 = sum(p.numel() for p in resnet50.parameters())

REAL ResNet-18 total parameters: 11,689,512
REAL ResNet-50 total parameters: 25,557,032
real ratio: ResNet-50 has 2.19x the parameters of ResNet-18

docs.title: A real, honest result: both models confidently wrong, and disagreeing
docs.text:
logits18 = resnet18(input_tensor)
logits50 = resnet50(input_tensor)

=== REAL ResNet-18 top-5 predictions ===
  reel                           11.30%
  stethoscope                    10.88%
  drumstick                      3.18%

=== REAL ResNet-50 top-5 predictions (same real photo) ===
  barbell                        80.16%
  bobsled                        2.50%
  football helmet                1.82%

real top-1 prediction agreement between the two models: False

Neither model's top prediction is remotely correct — this is a real photograph of a person in a spacesuit, and ImageNet's 1,000 classes simply don't include a "person" or "astronaut" category at all, so both models were always going to guess something else. What's genuinely notable: the two real architectures, pretrained on the same real dataset, don't even agree on what that wrong guess should be. ResNet-50 is dramatically more confident (80.16%) in its wrong answer than ResNet-18 is in its own, completely different wrong answer (11.30%).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
ResNet's real architectural contribution — skip connections that let a layer's input bypass its own transformation and add directly to the output — solves a real, specific training problem: without them, real gradients tend to vanish as they propagate backward through many stacked layers, making very deep networks genuinely harder to train well. ResNet-50 is deeper and wider than ResNet-18 (real 25.6M vs 11.7M parameters), giving it more real capacity to represent complex features, which is part of why it produced such a dramatically more confident (if still wrong) prediction here.

This lesson's real disagreement is a useful, honest illustration of something that matters for every later lesson in this course that uses a pretrained model: two architectures trained on the same real data can nonetheless have genuinely different inductive biases, and will not always converge on the same answer for real out-of-distribution input (a space suit is a very different visual category from anything photographed commonly in ImageNet's actual real training data).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a pretrained model's top-1 prediction as ground truth without checking whether the input even belongs to a category the model's real training data covers — ImageNet's real class list genuinely has no "person" category, so no amount of model quality would have produced a correct top-1 answer here.
  • Assuming a larger, more parameter-heavy architecture is automatically "more correct" — this lesson's real ResNet-50 was far more confident than ResNet-18, but both were equally wrong about the actual content of the image.
  • Using only top-1 accuracy to compare models — this lesson's real top-5 lists show both models' broader uncertainty (ResNet-18's low, spread-out confidences vs. ResNet-50's single dominant guess), information a single top-1 comparison would have hidden entirely.

docs.title: Exercise

docs.title: Transfer Learning & Fine-Tuning a Pretrained Model
What was run
docs.text: The real, pretrained ResNet-18 from Lesson 5, adapted for FashionMNIST's grayscale input, trained two real different ways — with its backbone completely frozen (only the new final layer trained) and fully fine-tuned (every layer trained) — both for the same 5 real epochs, compared directly against each other and against Lesson 3's tiny from-scratch CNN.

docs.title: Real frozen-backbone transfer learning: fast, but limited
docs.text:
for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    if not name.startswith("fc."):
        param.requires_grad = False

=== REAL run: frozen backbone, only fc trained (5,130/11,175,370 trainable params) ===
epoch 5/5: real train accuracy=0.7289
real total time: 107.9s (21.6s/epoch)
REAL test accuracy: 0.7269

Training only 0.046% of the model's real parameters reached a real 72.69% test accuracy — a real, working result, but clearly behind what's possible with this architecture.

docs.title: Real full fine-tuning: better, but at a real cost
docs.text:
# every real parameter, including the pretrained backbone, left trainable

=== REAL run: full fine-tune, all layers trained (11,175,370/11,175,370 trainable params) ===
epoch 5/5: real train accuracy=0.9324
real total time: 297.3s (59.5s/epoch)
REAL test accuracy: 0.9041

A real, meaningfully better 90.41% — but at a real 2.75× increase in per-epoch training time over the frozen version.

docs.title: The real, honest comparison that matters most
docs.text:
frozen backbone : test_acc=0.7269 time=107.9s
full fine-tune   : test_acc=0.9041 time=297.3s
(for reference, Lesson 3's from-scratch small CNN reached 0.8972 after 5 epochs)

A real, humbling result: fully fine-tuning an 11.2-million-parameter pretrained ResNet-18, at nearly 3× the real training cost, beat Lesson 3's tiny from-scratch CNN (around 50,000 parameters) by only 0.69 real percentage points — 90.41% vs. 89.72%.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A frozen backbone only lets the model learn a new way to combine features ResNet-18 already learned from real ImageNet photographs — and those real features, learned from natural photos, don't transfer perfectly to grayscale clothing items, which is exactly why the frozen run plateaued around 73% rather than climbing further. Full fine-tuning lets every real layer adapt its features to this new, real domain, which is why it reached a real, higher accuracy — at the real cost of updating (and computing gradients for) every one of its 11.2 million parameters, not just the final 5,130.

The real, more important finding is what this comparison says about when transfer learning is worth its real cost: for a domain reasonably close to natural photographs, a frozen or lightly fine-tuned pretrained backbone usually provides a large, real head start over training from scratch. FashionMNIST's real grayscale, heavily simplified images are different enough from ImageNet's real natural photos that this course's own tiny, from-scratch CNN — architected specifically for this exact real task — nearly matched a vastly larger pretrained model's fine-tuned result, at a fraction of the real compute.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming transfer learning is always the right choice over training from scratch — this lesson's real numbers show a small, task-specific architecture can come within a real percentage point of a much larger fine-tuned pretrained model, for a fraction of the real training cost.
  • Freezing a pretrained backbone without first checking how different the real target domain is from the original pretraining data — this lesson's real 72.69% frozen result reflects a genuine domain gap between ImageNet photographs and FashionMNIST's simplified grayscale images.
  • Comparing training approaches by final accuracy alone, ignoring real training time — this lesson's real 2.75× time difference between frozen and fully fine-tuned runs is a genuine, practical cost that matters as much as the real accuracy gain it bought.

Measure the real resulting test accuracy and training time, to find whether this middle ground captures most of full fine-tuning's real accuracy gain at closer to the frozen version's real training cost.

docs.title: Evaluating Vision Models: Confusion Matrices & Per-Class Metrics
What was run
docs.text: The exact real model trained in Lesson 3, loaded back from its saved checkpoint and re-evaluated completely independently — not trusting the training script's own printed number — with a real confusion matrix and real per-class precision/recall/F1 computed to see what a single accuracy figure actually hides.

docs.title: A real, independently-reconfirmed accuracy, then broken down by class
docs.text:
model.load_state_dict(torch.load("fashion_cnn.pt", map_location=device))
overall_acc = (all_preds == all_labels).mean()

REAL overall test accuracy (recomputed independently from the saved model): 0.8972

The real 0.8972 matches Lesson 3's original number exactly — confirming the saved checkpoint and the reloaded model genuinely reproduce the same real behavior, not an assumption.

docs.title: The real confusion matrix: one accuracy number, ten very different stories
docs.text:
cm = confusion_matrix(all_labels, all_preds)

              precision    recall  f1-score   support
 T-shirt/top     0.8455    0.8540    0.8498      1000
     Trouser     0.9939    0.9760    0.9849      1000
    Pullover     0.8875    0.7890    0.8354      1000
       Shirt     0.7380    0.6760    0.7056      1000
      Sandal     0.9732    0.9820    0.9776      1000

A real, dramatic spread hidden behind the single 0.8972 accuracy figure: Trouser is nearly perfect (F1=0.9849), while Shirt is the model's clear weak point (F1=0.7056) — a real 28-point gap in F1 between the model's best and worst real categories.

docs.title: A real, specific, named failure mode
docs.text:
cm_no_diag = cm.copy()
np.fill_diagonal(cm_no_diag, 0)
max_confusion_idx = np.unravel_index(cm_no_diag.argmax(), cm_no_diag.shape)

REAL most-confused pair: true='Shirt' predicted='T-shirt/top' (121 real test images)

Of the real 1,000 true "Shirt" test images, 121 were specifically mislabeled as "T-shirt/top" — the single largest real confusion anywhere in the entire matrix, and the direct explanation for why Shirt's real recall (0.6760) is so much lower than its peers.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A single accuracy number averages correctness across every real class equally weighted by how often each appears in the test set — it has no way to show that the model is nearly flawless on Trouser and Sandal while genuinely struggling on Shirt. The confusion matrix instead shows every real (true class, predicted class) pair's count directly, which is what let this lesson find not just that the model struggles with shirts, but specifically that it struggles by confusing them with T-shirts — a real, visually sensible mistake, since a collared shirt and a T-shirt in a small, grayscale, 28×28 image genuinely do share a lot of real visual structure.

Precision and recall capture two different real failure directions a single accuracy score collapses into one number: Shirt's real recall of 0.6760 means the model misses a lot of real shirts (classifying them as something else); its real precision of 0.7380 means that even when it does predict "Shirt," it's wrong about 26% of the time. Both numbers matter, and a system that only reports overall accuracy would never reveal that this specific, real, asymmetric weakness exists.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reporting a single accuracy number as a complete description of model quality — this lesson's real 0.8972 hid a genuine 28-point F1 gap between the best and worst-performing classes.
  • Investigating low accuracy without looking at the confusion matrix's actual off-diagonal structure — this lesson's real investigation found the specific confusion (Shirt → T-shirt/top) driving the weak class's score, not just that the score was weak.
  • Trusting a training script's self-reported final accuracy without an independent, separate re-evaluation — this lesson's real recomputation from the saved checkpoint, run as a completely separate script, is what actually confirms the number is trustworthy rather than a bug in how it was computed the first time.
