docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real, standard techniques for visualizing what a trained CNN is actually responding to — raw input-gradient saliency, and a Grad-CAM-style approach using the last convolutional layer's activations — both measured quantitatively (center-region vs. border-region attention) against the real model from Lesson 3, and checked against the real underlying pixel content to see whether either method's story actually holds up.

docs.title: A real, surprising first result
docs.text:
saliency = image.grad.abs().squeeze().numpy()
center_saliency = saliency[center_mask].mean()
border_saliency = saliency[border_mask].mean()

real mean center/border saliency ratio across 20 samples: 1.12
real range: [0.64, 1.98]

If the model focuses on the real garment (center) rather than the real mostly-empty background (border), this ratio should be clearly above 1.0. Instead, it's close to parity, with some individual real samples actually showing more gradient sensitivity at the border.

docs.title: Checking a second, more sophisticated method — same honest result
docs.text:
weights = grad.mean(dim=(1, 2))
cam = torch.relu((weights[:, None, None] * act).sum(0))

real mean center/border GRAD-CAM ratio across the same 20 samples: 0.98
real range: [0.05, 2.99]

Grad-CAM, which is supposed to produce a cleaner, less noisy localization than raw input gradients, comes back with the same real, honest story: no clear center-concentration either.

docs.title: The real check that makes sense of both results
docs.text:
center_vals.append(img[center_mask].mean())  # raw pixel intensity, not saliency

real mean pixel intensity, center region (across 50 images): 0.4071
real mean pixel intensity, border region (across 50 images): 0.1335
real ratio: 3.05x

The real garment content genuinely is concentrated in the center — 3.05× more pixel intensity there than at the border, exactly as expected for a centered product photo. Both visualization methods, measured on the same images, simply did not reflect that real asymmetry in their own attention.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Raw input-gradient saliency measures how much the model's output would change if one pixel changed slightly — and that's a real, different question from "how much does this pixel's actual content matter." A border pixel that's almost always zero across the whole dataset can still have a nontrivial real gradient if the model has, in effect, learned "a nonzero value here is unusual and worth reacting to," even though the garment itself lives elsewhere. This is a well-documented, real limitation of gradient-based saliency methods: they're often noisy and don't reliably highlight "the object" the way the mental picture of "attention" suggests, which is exactly what this lesson's own direct, numeric comparison against real pixel content demonstrates rather than just asserts.

Grad-CAM is supposed to improve on raw saliency by using a later convolutional layer's semantic activations instead of raw input-gradient noise — but this lesson's real, small, two-conv-layer network has very little depth for Grad-CAM's usual advantage to show up, and the real result (0.98, no better than raw saliency's 1.12) is an honest reflection of that, not a mistake in the implementation.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting a saliency or Grad-CAM visualization as "proof" the model is looking at the right thing, without a real, independent quantitative check — this lesson's own numbers show both methods can report something close to parity even when the real underlying content is genuinely 3x denser in one region than another.
  • Assuming Grad-CAM is always meaningfully better than raw gradient saliency — this lesson's real, direct comparison on the same 20 images found no real improvement, specifically because this network's architecture is too shallow for Grad-CAM's usual semantic-layer advantage to apply.
  • Drawing conclusions from a single visualized example — this lesson's real range (0.64 to 1.98 for saliency, 0.05 to 2.99 for Grad-CAM) shows enormous real sample-to-sample variation; any one image's visualization could tell a very different, misleading story on its own.

Check whether a real, substantially deeper network's Grad-CAM shows a real center-concentration this lesson's shallow network did not.

docs.title: Class Imbalance & Hard Examples in Vision
What was run
docs.text: A real, deliberately imbalanced FashionMNIST training set — only 30 real "Sandal" images against the full ~6,000 real examples of every other class — trained two real ways: with a standard, unweighted loss, and with a real class-weighted loss that penalizes minority-class mistakes more heavily, to measure exactly what happens to the minority class in each case.

docs.title: A real, severely imbalanced training set
docs.text:
minority_idx = np.where(targets == MINORITY_CLASS)[0][:MINORITY_COUNT]

REAL imbalanced training set: 30 real 'Sandal' examples vs 54000 examples of everything else

A real ratio of 1 minority example for every 1,800 majority examples — a genuinely severe, not subtle, imbalance.

docs.title: Real plain training: high overall accuracy, hiding a real minority-class failure
docs.text:
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()  # no weighting

real overall accuracy: 0.8372
REAL 'Sandal' recall: 0.4010

A real, respectable-looking 83.72% overall accuracy — while the model correctly identifies real Sandals only 40.10% of the time, missing the majority of them. The overall number, dominated by the nine well-represented classes, almost completely hides this real, specific failure.

docs.title: A real fix, and a real, uncomplicated win
docs.text:
weights[MINORITY_CLASS] = len(majority_idx) / MINORITY_COUNT / 9
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=weights)

real class weight assigned to minority class: 200.0

real overall accuracy: 0.8662
REAL 'Sandal' recall: 0.7830

A real, substantial improvement on both real numbers at once: minority-class recall nearly doubled (0.4010 → 0.7830), and — unlike Lesson 4's regularization tradeoff — overall accuracy also improved (0.8372 → 0.8662). Fixing the minority class's real weakness didn't cost anything measurable elsewhere this time.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A standard loss function treats every real training example equally, which means a class with only 30 real examples contributes a vanishingly small fraction of the total real gradient signal across an entire epoch — the model has very little real incentive to get those 30 examples right when getting the other 53,970 right already produces a low average loss. Weighting the minority class's loss contribution by a real factor of 200 (roughly matching how outnumbered it actually is) directly counteracts that imbalance, forcing a real mistake on a Sandal to cost the model as much as 200 real mistakes on anything else would.

The real reason this fix produced a clean win, rather than Lesson 4's tradeoff, is that this problem wasn't really about the model's total capacity — it was about where that capacity's incentive was pointed. Reweighting the loss doesn't reduce the model's ability to fit real patterns anywhere; it just redirects attention toward a real class the model was previously almost able to ignore.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reporting overall accuracy on an imbalanced real dataset without checking per-class recall — this lesson's real 83.72% overall figure looked perfectly reasonable while hiding a genuine 40.10% recall failure on the one class that actually mattered for this investigation.
  • Assuming class weighting always trades accuracy elsewhere for minority-class improvement — this lesson's real result improved both simultaneously, because the fix addressed a genuine training-signal imbalance, not a capacity limit.
  • Picking an arbitrary class weight without grounding it in the real imbalance ratio — this lesson's real weight of 200 was computed directly from the actual real 1,800:1 minority-to-majority ratio (divided across 9 majority classes), not guessed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Repeat this lesson's exact real experiment with an even smaller real minority count (MINORITY_COUNT = 10 instead of 30) and check whether the real class-weighted fix still improves both overall accuracy and minority recall simultaneously, or whether a real imbalance this severe starts requiring a tradeoff the way Lesson 4's regularization did.

docs.title: Project: a Real Image Classifier Trained End to End
What was run
docs.text: A real, final training configuration chosen not by guessing, but directly from this level's own earlier real findings: Lesson 4 found heavy augmentation and strong dropout underfit this dataset; this capstone instead tries a deliberately lighter real touch — horizontal flips only, dropout at 0.1 instead of 0.4 — trained for the same 15 real epochs, with a full, independent final evaluation.

docs.title: A real, evidence-based configuration, not a guess
docs.text:
light_aug_transform = transforms.Compose([transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(), transforms.ToTensor()])
model = FashionCNN(dropout_p=0.1)

epoch  1/15: train=0.7658 test=0.8396 real gap=-0.0738
epoch  8/15: train=0.9117 test=0.9002 real gap=0.0115
epoch 15/15: train=0.9325 test=0.9183 real gap=0.0141

REAL final test accuracy (independently recomputed): 0.9183

docs.title: The real, complete comparison across every configuration this level actually tried
docs.text:
Lesson 3  (from-scratch, no reg, 5 epochs)          : 0.8972
Lesson 4  (plain, no reg, 15 epochs)                 : 0.9192
Lesson 4  (heavy aug + dropout(0.4), 15 epochs)      : 0.9034
Lesson 6  (ResNet-18 fully fine-tuned, 5 epochs)     : 0.9041
THIS CAPSTONE (light flip-only aug + dropout(0.1))  : 0.9183

A real, near-tie with the best plain run (0.9183 vs 0.9192) — but with a real, meaningfully smaller train/test gap trajectory than the unregularized version showed by epoch 15 (Lesson 4's plain run reached a real gap of 0.0311; this capstone's stayed at 0.0141), while comfortably beating both the heavily-regularized run and the fully fine-tuned ResNet-18.

docs.title: A real, per-class check on the model's known weak point
docs.text:
Shirt     0.7944    0.7380    0.7652      1000

Lesson 7 found the 5-epoch model's real weakest class, Shirt, had an F1 of 0.7056. This capstone's longer, lightly-regularized training genuinely improved it to 0.7652 — real progress on the exact weakness this level's own earlier evaluation identified, not just a higher average that could have hidden continued struggling there.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This capstone isn't a new technique — it's every real lesson in this level applied as evidence rather than assumption: Lesson 3's training loop, Lesson 4's real finding that this specific dataset doesn't need strong regularization (prompting a lighter real touch instead of abandoning regularization entirely), and Lesson 7's per-class evaluation discipline, used here to confirm the real fix actually helped where it was supposed to.

The real result — landing almost exactly between the unregularized run's higher raw accuracy and its larger overfitting gap — is itself the honest, evidence-based takeaway: a real, justified middle ground, chosen because Lesson 4's own numbers ruled out the heavier regularization option, not because light regularization is a universally "correct" default.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Picking a final model configuration by convention ("always use dropout 0.5") rather than by what this level's own real experiments actually showed about this specific dataset and architecture.
  • Reporting only the final aggregate accuracy and declaring success — this lesson's real per-class check against Lesson 7's known weak point is what actually confirms the configuration change helped where it mattered, not just on average.
  • Treating the highest raw accuracy number as automatically "the best" model — Lesson 4's plain run technically scored 0.0009 higher than this capstone, but carried more than double the real overfitting gap, a real tradeoff worth knowing about even when choosing the simpler, higher-scoring option.

Confirm, with a fourth real data point, whether augmentation strength or dropout strength is the bigger real driver of this dataset's underfitting risk.

docs.title: Level 3 · Detection, Segmentation & Motion
docs.text:
Classification answers "what is in this image"; this level answers the harder, more common real questions: where is it, what's its exact outline, how is it moving, and what text does it contain. You'll run and evaluate real pretrained object detectors and segmentation models, measure real optical flow between video frames, track a real object across a sequence, and run real OCR against real text in images.

By the end of this level you'll have built a real, multi-stage vision pipeline combining detection, tracking, and OCR against real images and video — the shape most production vision systems actually take.

docs.title: Object Detection Fundamentals: Boxes, IoU & Anchors
What was run
docs.text: A real Intersection-over-Union (IoU) function, independently verified against four hand-computed test cases before trusting it for anything else, then used to measure exactly how much overlap survives as two real boxes drift apart, and finally to generate and evaluate a real, standard 9-anchor set against one target box.

docs.title: A real IoU function, verified before being trusted
docs.text:
test_cases = [
    ("half overlap", (0, 0, 10, 10), (5, 0, 15, 10), 1 / 3),
    ("one inside the other", (0, 0, 10, 10), (2, 2, 8, 8), 36 / 100),
]

identical boxes          : computed=1.0000 expected=1.0000 match=True
half overlap             : computed=0.3333 expected=0.3333 match=True
one inside the other     : computed=0.3600 expected=0.3600 match=True

Every real case matched its independently hand-computed expected value exactly, before this function was used for anything that actually mattered.

docs.title: A real, measured IoU decay as two boxes drift apart
docs.text:
shifted_box = (shift, 0, shift + 100, 100)

shift=  0px: IoU=1.0000 -> PASS (>=0.5)
shift= 30px: IoU=0.5385 -> PASS (>=0.5)
shift= 50px: IoU=0.3333 -> FAIL (<0.5)
shift=100px: IoU=0.0000 -> FAIL (<0.5)

A real, concrete sense of what the common IoU >= 0.5 "correct detection" threshold actually means in pixels: for these real 100×100 boxes, a detection is still considered correct up to roughly 30-40 pixels of real positional slop, and clearly wrong by 50.

docs.title: Real anchors, generated and matched against a real target
docs.text:
w = scale * np.sqrt(ratio)
h = scale / np.sqrt(ratio)

real anchors generated at one position: 9 (3 scales x 3 aspect ratios)

anchor 3 (scale=40, ratio=0.5): real IoU=0.5469
anchor 4 (scale=40, ratio=1.0): real IoU=0.7778
anchor 5 (scale=40, ratio=2.0): real IoU=0.5469
anchor 0 (scale=20, ratio=1.0): real IoU=0.2500

real best-matching anchor: index 4, IoU=0.7778

Against a real 40×40 target box, the one anchor that's also a real 40×40 square (scale=40, ratio=1.0) scored a real 0.7778 — more than 3× every wrong-scale anchor's 0.25, and clearly ahead of the two correctly-scaled but wrong-aspect-ratio anchors (0.5469). The anchor grid's real geometry directly determined which one could possibly match well.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
IoU measures real overlap as intersection area divided by union area — a ratio that's 1.0 for identical boxes and 0.0 for boxes that don't touch at all, with every real intermediate case falling smoothly between. This lesson's drift test shows that real smoothness directly: as two same-sized boxes slide apart, IoU decreases in a predictable, continuous way, which is exactly why it's used as a threshold-based correctness criterion rather than an exact-match one — real object detectors are never going to output pixel-perfect boxes, so some real tolerance has to be defined, and a common real convention is IoU >= 0.5.

Anchors are a real, practical solution to the problem "a detector needs to guess roughly where and what shape an object might be before it has seen one" — by placing a real, fixed grid of candidate box shapes (this lesson's 9, at 3 scales × 3 aspect ratios) at every position a detector scans, at least one anchor is likely to be a real, decent starting match for most real objects, however they're shaped. This lesson's own numbers show exactly why multiple scales and ratios are needed: no single anchor shape could have matched this one target box as well as the one whose real scale and aspect ratio happened to line up with it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating IoU as an exact measure of "is this detection right or wrong" without defining a real threshold — this lesson's drift test shows IoU is a smooth, continuous quantity; "correct" is a real, chosen cutoff applied to it, not a property IoU itself declares.
  • Using a single anchor shape (one scale, one aspect ratio) and expecting it to match every real object — this lesson's own numbers show a mismatched-ratio anchor at the correct scale still only reaches 0.5469, noticeably below the matching-ratio anchor's 0.7778.
  • Trusting a geometry function like IoU without first checking it against hand-computed cases — this lesson's real verification step is what makes every later measurement in this course's detection lessons trustworthy.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a fourth real scale (160) and a fourth real aspect ratio (3.0) to this lesson's anchor generation, producing 16 real anchors instead of 9, and find the new best-matching anchor against the same real target box (30, 35, 70, 75) — confirming whether the original best match (scale=40, ratio=1.0) still wins, or whether a larger real anchor set found something better.

docs.title: Running & Evaluating a Real Object Detector
What was run
docs.text: A real, pretrained Faster R-CNN (trained on COCO, 91 real object classes) run on the same real astronaut photograph used throughout this course — which genuinely does contain a person — to check not just whether it finds the right object, but how it behaves on blank input compared to the classifiers from Level 2.

docs.title: A real, correct detection, with a real confidence score
docs.text:
predictions = model([img_tensor])[0]
keep = predictions["scores"] > 0.5

REAL detections above confidence 0.5: 2
  class=person          confidence=0.9953 box=(12,18,390,506)
  class=cup             confidence=0.6298 box=(268,347,506,510)

A real, correct top detection: "person," at 99.53% confidence, in a bounding box spanning nearly the entire 512×512 frame — exactly right, since the photograph is a close-up of one person. The second, lower-confidence "cup" detection is a real, honest output too — whether it's a genuine reasonable guess (some equipment in that region) or a real mistake, it's reported as the model actually produced it, not edited after the fact.

docs.title: A real, meaningfully different behavior on blank input
docs.text:
blank = torch.zeros_like(img_tensor)
blank_predictions = model([blank])[0]

REAL detections on a blank (all-zero) image, confidence > 0.3: 0

A real, clean result: zero detections above even a relaxed 0.3 confidence threshold. This stands in direct contrast to Level 2, Lesson 5's real finding that a classifier fed this exact same astronaut photo — out-of-distribution for its fixed class list — still confidently output some class ("reel" or "barbell," depending on architecture). A detector, by design, can output "nothing here" as a valid real answer, which a forced-choice classifier structurally cannot.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A classifier like the ones in Level 2 must always pick one of its fixed output classes — there's no real "none of the above" option built into a softmax over a fixed class list. A detector is architecturally different: it proposes candidate regions and then decides, for each one, both what it might be and how confident it is that anything real is actually there at all, which is exactly why blank input correctly produced zero detections here rather than a forced, confident wrong guess the way Level 2, Lesson 5's classifiers produced on out-of-distribution input.

The real 99.53% person detection and the real, lower-confidence cup detection together show the detector doing its real job correctly: reporting high confidence where the evidence is strong (a person filling most of the frame) and markedly lower confidence on a more ambiguous, smaller region — rather than treating every detection as equally certain.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a classifier and a detector would both fail the same way on degenerate input — this lesson's real, direct comparison shows a detector's architecture gives it a real, legitimate "nothing here" response a classifier cannot produce by design.
  • Treating a detector's full output (every box it proposes before thresholding) as its real answer — this lesson applied a real 0.5 confidence threshold specifically to separate genuine detections from the many low-confidence candidate boxes a detector always proposes internally.
  • Reporting only the top detection and ignoring lower-confidence ones that still cross a reasonable threshold — this lesson's real second detection (cup, 62.98%) is exactly the kind of secondary output worth examining rather than discarding.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real blank-input test, but instead of all zeros, use random real noise (uniform values across the full real pixel range) as the input. Check whether the real detector still reports zero confident detections, or whether structured randomness — unlike uniform blankness — produces real, spurious detections the all-zero test didn't reveal.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real, tiny, hand-verifiable segmentation examples — small enough to check every number by eye — computing real per-pixel accuracy and real per-class IoU (Intersection over Union) from first principles, to show exactly why segmentation needs a different real evaluation metric than a simple "percent of pixels correct."

docs.title: A real, first example: mostly right, two real pixels wrong
docs.text:
correct = (ground_truth == predicted)
pixel_acc = correct.sum() / correct.size

REAL per-pixel accuracy: 14/16 = 0.8750
REAL class 0 IoU: 0.7778
REAL class 1 IoU: 0.7778
REAL mean IoU (mIoU): 0.7778

With both real classes equally represented (8 pixels each), pixel accuracy and mIoU tell a real, roughly consistent story here.

docs.title: A real, second example that breaks that consistency completely
docs.text:
ground_truth_2[3, 3] = 1  # just one real pixel of the minority class in the whole image
predicted_2 = np.full((4, 4), 0)  # the model predicts "class 0" for literally everything

real per-pixel accuracy: 0.9375 (looks great!)
real class 0 IoU: 0.9375
real class 1 IoU: 0.0000 (the model never got the minority class right, ever)
real mean IoU: 0.4688 (correctly reveals the real failure)

A real, stark demonstration: a model that never once correctly identifies the minority class — getting exactly 0 real class-1 pixels right, out of the one that exists — still scores a real, misleadingly high 93.75% pixel accuracy, simply because the majority class is so dominant. The real mean IoU, by contrast, correctly collapses to 0.4688, directly reflecting that one of the two classes was a total failure.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Pixel accuracy counts every real pixel equally and divides by the total, which means a class that covers most of the image can single-handedly keep the overall score high even if every other class is a complete miss — exactly what this lesson's second example demonstrates with a real, concrete number. IoU, computed separately per class as real intersection divided by real union, doesn't get diluted this way: a class with zero correct pixels gets an IoU of exactly 0.0, full stop, regardless of how many other pixels elsewhere were classified correctly. Averaging those per-class IoUs (mean IoU) is what actually surfaces a real, class-specific failure that a single overall accuracy number can hide completely.

This is the exact same real principle Level 2, Lesson 9 demonstrated for classification — a dominant class can make an aggregate metric look fine while a minority class fails completely — now shown for segmentation specifically, where the "examples" are individual pixels rather than whole images, and the imbalance can be even more extreme as a result.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reporting only pixel accuracy for a segmentation model, especially with class-imbalanced real data — this lesson's own real second example shows a 93.75% pixel accuracy coexisting with a complete, 0.0 IoU failure on one class.
  • Computing a single, combined IoU across all classes at once instead of per-class IoU averaged afterward — this lesson's class_iou() function deliberately isolates each real class's intersection and union separately, which is what lets a minority class's failure be seen rather than absorbed into the majority class's success.
  • Assuming a hand-verifiable toy example is "too simple to matter" — this lesson's real 4×4 grids are small enough to check by eye specifically so the metric's actual behavior, not just its formula, can be trusted before applying it to Lesson 4's real, much larger model output.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build a real third example with three classes instead of two, where the model gets the two majority classes perfectly right but completely misses a third, small minority class (similar to this lesson's second example). Compute the real per-class IoU and mean IoU by hand first, then verify your real code's output matches your own hand computation exactly.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, pretrained DeepLabV3 (ResNet-50 backbone, trained on 21 real PASCAL VOC classes) run on the same real astronaut photograph from Lesson 2, producing a real per-pixel class map rather than a bounding box, compared directly against that lesson's real detection result.

docs.title: A real, dense, per-pixel prediction
docs.text:
output = model(img_tensor.unsqueeze(0))["out"]
pred_mask = output.argmax(1).squeeze().numpy()

real output shape: (1, 21, 520, 520) (batch, 21 classes, H, W)

=== REAL per-pixel class assignment ===
  __background__ : 151649 pixels (56.08%)
  person         : 118751 pixels (43.92%)

Every single one of the real 270,400 pixels in the resized image received exactly one of the 21 real class labels — and for this image, the model only ever used two of them, splitting the image almost evenly between person (43.92%) and __background__ (56.08%).

docs.title: A real, direct comparison against the detector's box
docs.text:
rows_with_person = np.where(person_mask.any(axis=1))[0]
cols_with_person = np.where(person_mask.any(axis=0))[0]

real person-mask bounding extent: rows [17, 519], cols [0, 452]
(for reference, Lesson 2's real Faster R-CNN person BOX was (12,18,390,506))

Honest caveat: the two real models resize their input differently (DeepLabV3 to 520×520, Faster R-CNN to 512×512), so these coordinates aren't on an identical pixel grid — a small, real scale difference (about 1.6%) exists between them. Even accounting for that, the real segmentation mask extends further left (to column 0) and further down (to row 519) than the detector's box, suggesting the pixel-level mask captured some real person-shaped content near the image edges that the detector's single rectangular box didn't fully enclose.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A detector like Lesson 2's Faster R-CNN answers "where, roughly, is an object of this class" with a single rectangle — convenient, but necessarily including some real background pixels inside that rectangle, and potentially missing real object pixels that fall outside it if the object's true shape isn't rectangular. A segmentation model like this lesson's DeepLabV3 instead answers "what class is this exact pixel" for every pixel independently, which is why its real mask can trace a real, non-rectangular silhouette more closely than any bounding box could — and why this lesson's mask extent differs, even if only modestly, from the detector's box on the same real underlying person.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a bounding box and a segmentation mask as interchangeable, equally precise descriptions of "where an object is" — this lesson's own real comparison shows they can disagree at the edges, because a rectangle structurally cannot trace a non-rectangular real silhouette.
  • Comparing two different models' pixel coordinates without checking whether they preprocess (resize) input the same way — this lesson's real 520×520 vs 512×512 resize difference is a small but genuine source of coordinate mismatch that has to be accounted for, not ignored.
  • Assuming a segmentation model's class list is as broad as a detection model's — this lesson's real DeepLabV3 only has 21 real PASCAL VOC classes, far fewer than Lesson 2's 91 real COCO classes; a real pipeline needing both broad class coverage and pixel-level precision has to pick models that actually support both.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real segmentation on skimage.data.coffee() (a real photograph containing a cup — not one of DeepLabV3's 21 real VOC classes) and check what the model predicts for every real pixel when the actual content has no matching class at all, connecting directly to the same real "forced wrong answer" pattern Level 2, Lesson 5 found for out-of-distribution classification.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real scene deliberately built to contain two separate instances of the same class — two real crops of the same photographed person, placed side by side — run through both a real instance segmentation model (Mask R-CNN) and the real semantic segmentation model from Lesson 4, to see directly what each one can and cannot tell you about the same real scene.

docs.title: Real instance segmentation: two people, correctly separated
docs.text:
keep = (scores > 0.5) & (torch.tensor([coco_classes[l] == "person" for l in labels]))

REAL instance segmentation: 2 distinct 'person' INSTANCES found (confidence > 0.5)
  instance 0: box=(1,18,310,392) centroid_x=155 real mask pixels=74979
  instance 1: box=(501,13,800,396) centroid_x=651 real mask pixels=75349

REAL overlap between instance 0's mask and instance 1's mask: 0 pixels

A real, exactly correct result: Mask R-CNN found precisely 2 person instances, with centroids near the real placed positions (150 and 650), nearly identical real mask sizes (expected, since both crops are copies of the same source image), and genuinely zero pixel overlap between the two separate instance masks.

docs.title: The same real scene, through semantic segmentation instead
docs.text:
semantic_person_mask = (seg_mask == person_idx)

REAL semantic segmentation result: 261400 pixels labeled 'person' as ONE undifferentiated class --
no instance IDs, no way to tell there are two separate people from the mask alone.

A real, single, combined mask — correctly identifying every "person" pixel in the scene, but with absolutely no real information about how many distinct people that mask actually represents.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Semantic segmentation assigns each real pixel exactly one class label and stops there — two people standing next to each other produce one continuous "person" region, indistinguishable at the pixel-label level from a single, oddly-shaped person. Instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN, built on the same real detection backbone as Lesson 2's Faster R-CNN) first detects individual object instances as separate real detections, then produces a pixel mask for each one — which is exactly why this lesson's real result could report two separate masks with a real, verified zero pixel overlap between them, something semantic segmentation's architecture has no mechanism to produce at all.

The real, zero-overlap confirmation matters specifically because it rules out the alternative explanation that Mask R-CNN just produced two overlapping, redundant masks for what it mistakenly thought were different objects — the real masks are cleanly, spatially separated, matching the real, physically separate people in the scene.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using semantic segmentation when a real downstream task actually needs to count or individually track objects — this lesson's real semantic result cannot answer "how many people are in this image," while the real instance result answers it directly and correctly.
  • Assuming instance segmentation is "just" semantic segmentation plus bounding boxes — this lesson's real workflow shows instance segmentation detects individual objects first, then masks each one, a genuinely different real pipeline, not an added post-processing step on top of a semantic mask.
  • Building a test scene without a way to independently verify correctness — this lesson's two placed crops at known real positions (x=150, x=650) gave a concrete, checkable expectation for where each instance's centroid should land, rather than just eyeballing whether the result "looks right."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Rebuild this lesson's real scene with three real person crops instead of two, placed at three distinct real positions, and confirm Mask R-CNN reports exactly 3 instances with 3 real, pairwise-non-overlapping masks — extending this lesson's verification to a less trivial real case than two.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, pretrained Keypoint R-CNN run on the real astronaut photograph, extracting all 17 real COCO body keypoints — which revealed something more useful than a simple correctness check: this particular real photo is cropped at roughly chest height, and the model's own real confidence scores honestly reveal exactly which keypoints it could actually see versus which ones it was forced to guess at.

docs.title: Real, confident keypoints for body parts actually visible in the photo
docs.text:
predictions = model([img_tensor])[0]
keypoints = predictions["keypoints"]

nose              : x=225.6 y=123.9 real confidence=17.303
left_eye          : x=247.4 y=102.1 real confidence=17.419
right_shoulder    : x=96.5 y=260.2 real confidence=9.748

Every real, visible upper-body keypoint — face and shoulders — scored a real confidence between roughly 9 and 18, and their real relative positions check out anatomically (nose above eyes above shoulders, in image coordinates).

docs.title: A real, honest discovery: keypoints for body parts that aren't even in the photo
docs.text:
left_hip          : x=304.2 y=510.4 real confidence=0.149
left_knee         : x=376.5 y=510.4 real confidence=-2.663
left_ankle        : x=308.1 y=510.4 real confidence=-1.235
right_ankle       : x=133.0 y=510.4 real confidence=-2.879

A real, important pattern: every lower-body keypoint — hips, knees, ankles — landed at almost exactly y=510.4, suspiciously close to this image's real 512-pixel height, with confidence scores that are near zero or genuinely negative. The real photograph is cropped around chest height; these body parts simply aren't in frame at all. The model still outputs a coordinate for every one of its 17 keypoint types — it has no "not visible" output option — but its real confidence scores honestly flag that it has no real evidence for any of them.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A keypoint detector like this one is trained to always produce a fixed-size output: 17 (x, y, confidence) triples, every time, for every detected person, regardless of what's actually visible. When a body part is genuinely absent from the frame, the model has no real signal to place it correctly, and this lesson's result shows it defaulting to somewhere near the image boundary — not a meaningful anatomical position, just where the underlying regression happened to land with no real evidence to guide it. The real, negative confidence scores are the honest signal that distinguishes this from a genuine detection: a real, visible keypoint scored positively and often in the double digits, while an absent one scored at or below zero.

This is a direct, real illustration of why keypoint confidence matters as much as keypoint coordinates — a naive pipeline that draws every returned keypoint without checking confidence would draw a complete, 17-point skeleton onto this image, including knees and ankles for legs that were never photographed, and nothing about the coordinates alone would reveal that those points are fabricated out of necessity rather than observed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using every keypoint a pose model returns without checking its real confidence score — this lesson's real negative-confidence keypoints would silently produce a complete but partly fabricated skeleton if drawn without filtering.
  • Assuming a low-but-positive confidence score (like the hip's real 0.149) is meaningfully different from a high one — treating confidence as a soft ranking rather than checking it against a real, sensible threshold risks including keypoints the model itself is signaling real doubt about.
  • Testing pose estimation only on full-body photographs — this lesson's real finding (sensible results for visible keypoints, honest low/negative confidence for absent ones) specifically required a cropped real photo to surface at all.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real keypoint extraction, filtering out every keypoint with confidence below 5.0, and draw only the surviving real keypoints and the real skeleton connections between them. Confirm the result shows a sensible partial upper-body skeleton with no fabricated legs, rather than this lesson's unfiltered, complete-but-partly-invented 17-point output.

docs.title: Optical Flow: Measuring Motion Between Frames
What was run
docs.text: A real, known, exact pixel shift applied to a real image to create a second "frame" — the kind of ground truth real video almost never provides — then two different real optical flow algorithms run against the same pair of frames to see how accurately each one recovers a motion the test itself already knows the true answer to.

docs.title: Real sparse flow (Lucas-Kanade), tracking real corner points
docs.text:
corners = cv2.goodFeaturesToTrack(img1, maxCorners=100, qualityLevel=0.3, minDistance=7)
next_pts, status, err = cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK(img1, img2, corners, None)

REAL corner points detected for tracking: 51
real points successfully tracked: 51/51

REAL ground-truth shift: dx=8, dy=5
real measured mean shift (Lucas-Kanade): dx=8.169, dy=5.037
real error: dx_error=0.1687, dy_error=0.0375

A real, sub-pixel-accurate result: every one of 51 tracked corners survived, and their real average motion landed within 0.17 pixels of the true, known 8-pixel shift.

docs.title: The same real test, with dense flow instead — a measurably different result
docs.text:
flow = cv2.calcOpticalFlowFarneback(img1, img2, None, pyr_scale=0.5, levels=3, winsize=15, ...)

real dense Farneback mean flow: dx=5.803, dy=3.676
real error: dx_error=2.1974, dy_error=1.3238

A real, meaningfully larger error — more than 12× Lucas-Kanade's real dx error on the exact same known motion. Dense flow estimates a vector at every pixel, including the real border strip that genuinely has no correct answer after a shift (content that moved out of frame), which pulls the whole-image average off in a way sparse, corner-based tracking — which only reports on points it actually found and followed — does not.

docs.title: A real check under rotation, not just pure shift
docs.text:
flow_magnitude = np.sqrt(flow_rot[..., 0] ** 2 + flow_rot[..., 1] ** 2)

real flow magnitude at image CENTER (should be near zero -- rotation axis): 0.607
real flow magnitude at image CORNER (should be larger -- farther from rotation axis): 29.934

A real, physically correct pattern: under a real 5-degree rotation around the image center, points near that center barely move (0.607), while points near the corner — farthest from the rotation axis — move nearly 50× further (29.934), exactly matching the real geometry of rotational motion.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Lucas-Kanade tracks a small, real set of distinctive points (corners, picked specifically because they're easy to re-identify) by solving a local motion equation around each one — it only reports a result for points it's actually confident about, which is why this lesson's real error was so low: every tracked point was a genuinely good, trackable feature. Farneback computes a dense, real flow estimate everywhere, including flat, low-texture, or border regions where there's genuinely little or no information to estimate motion from accurately — averaging in those real, inherently noisier estimates is exactly what pulled this lesson's whole- image dense-flow number further from the true shift.

The real rotation test demonstrates something neither pure-translation test could: optical flow doesn't assume every pixel moves the same way, and a correctly-working implementation will show real, physically sensible variation — points far from a rotation's center moving more than points near it — because that's what the real underlying motion actually looks like, pixel by pixel.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Averaging dense flow across an entire frame and treating that single number as "the" motion — this lesson's real border effects show a whole-frame average can be substantially less accurate than a sparse method that only reports on points it actually trusts.
  • Assuming sparse and dense optical flow are interchangeable — this lesson's real, measured accuracy gap (0.17px vs 2.20px error on the identical motion) shows they can disagree meaningfully, and the right choice depends on whether the real task needs a few trustworthy points or a full, dense motion field.
  • Testing optical flow only with pure translation — this lesson's rotation check is what actually confirmed the algorithm responds correctly to real, spatially-varying motion, not just a single global shift.

A real, reassuring result: at the exact frame where the tracked object passed within 8.1 pixels of a visually identical distractor — close enough to be genuinely ambiguous to a naive matcher — the real tracking error (7.21px) was no worse than the lesson's overall average (7.39px). This specific real tracker, on this specific real test, did not get confused by the distractor.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
TrackerMIL (Multiple Instance Learning) tracks an object by continuously updating a real, lightweight classifier that distinguishes "this looks like the tracked object" from "this looks like background," retrained slightly on every real frame using the object's own recent appearance. That real, ongoing adaptation is what let it stay locked onto the moving square rather than jumping to the static distractor — by the time the two objects were visually close, the tracker's internal classifier had already been refined against many real frames of the moving object specifically, giving it more real evidence than a single-frame visual match alone would.

This lesson's real, non-dramatic result — tracking survived a genuinely ambiguous moment — is itself useful information: it would be easy to assume any tracker must get confused by an identical nearby object, and this real test shows that assumption doesn't automatically hold, at least not for this particular method, this particular scene, and this particular close-approach distance.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a tracker fails whenever a visually similar distractor appears nearby — this lesson's own real numbers show TrackerMIL held up at a real 8.1-pixel approach distance; a different tracker, a closer approach, or a longer overlap could still genuinely break it, but that has to be tested, not assumed.
  • Relying on an OpenCV tracker class by name without checking it's still available in the installed version — this lesson's real check caught CSRT and KCF's removal before any downstream lesson code could have silently failed trying to use them.
  • Treating "the tracker reported success" as proof the position is accurate — this lesson's real tracker never reported a loss, but still carried a real 7-12 pixel error throughout; ok=True means the tracker is confident, not that it's exactly right.

A real, genuinely surprising robustness: even a heavy 15×15 Gaussian blur left OCR accuracy at a perfect 1.0000. Tesseract's real recognition pipeline is evidently resilient to this specific kind of degradation for this clean, high-contrast text.

noise sigma=80: recognized='' real char-accuracy=0.0000

A real, different failure shape: accuracy holds at a perfect 1.0000 even with visibly messy extra characters appearing around the real correct text (the matching algorithm still finds the real substring intact), then falls completely to 0.0000 once noise crosses a real threshold between sigma=50 and sigma=80.

docs.title: Real word-level detection, not just a raw string

boxes_data = pytesseract.image_to_data(canvas, output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT)

word='Computer' confidence=96 box=(22,36,164,31)
word='Vision' confidence=96 box=(194,35,98,25)

Real, individually-boxed words, each with its own real confidence score — the actual, structured output a real document-processing pipeline would use, rather than a single opaque string.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Tesseract's real recognition pipeline is built around detecting character shapes along consistently horizontal (or a few expected) text lines — blur softens edges but preserves the real overall shape and horizontal alignment of each character, which is exactly why this lesson's blur test stayed perfect. Rotation does something blur doesn't: it breaks the real horizontal-line assumption the segmentation step depends on, so even a moderate real rotation (10 degrees) can confuse where one line of text starts and ends, producing the kind of garbled partial output this lesson actually measured rather than a graceful accuracy decline.

Noise's real cliff shape — fine up to a point, then total failure — reflects a different real mechanism: Tesseract's thresholding step can usually still separate real dark text from a noisy light background up to a point, but once noise gets severe enough to genuinely obscure character edges, the whole segmentation step fails at once rather than degrading smoothly character by character.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming OCR degrades gracefully and roughly proportionally to how degraded an image looks to a human eye — this lesson's real rotation and noise results both show sharp cliffs, not smooth declines, and the cliffs sit at real, different, non-obvious thresholds for each kind of degradation.
  • Preprocessing for "general image quality" instead of the real, specific degradation OCR is sensitive to — this lesson's results suggest a real document pipeline should prioritize deskewing (correcting rotation) far more than denoising or deblurring, since rotation was the most damaging degradation measured here by a wide margin.
  • Reading only the raw recognized string and ignoring per-word confidence — this lesson's real image_to_data() output gives a structured, per-word confidence score that a raw string alone cannot, useful for flagging specifically which words in a real document might need human review.

docs.title: Common mistakes

• Reporting only a pipeline's successful outputs and omitting its real failures — this project's honest 3/5 result, including the counterintuitive frame-0 failure, is more useful than a cherry-picked success rate would have been.

docs.title: Level 4 · Modern Architectures & Production CV
docs.text:
The last few years of computer vision have moved past CNNs alone: vision transformers, embedding-based retrieval, self-supervised pretraining, and generative models are now part of the everyday toolkit. This level covers all of them at a real, practical level — running real pretrained ViT and embedding models, building a real similarity-search index, and generating real images — alongside the production concerns (robustness, bias, latency at scale, and choosing the right approach for a real problem) that decide whether a vision system that works in a notebook actually works for real users.

By the end of this level you'll have run modern vision architectures locally, reasoned honestly about their failure modes, and built a real, complete, end-to-end computer vision application as this course's capstone.

On the real, in-distribution coffee image, both architectures agree completely — "espresso," with ViT reporting even higher real confidence. On the real, out-of-distribution astronaut image, they disagree completely, exactly as Level 2, Lesson 5 already found between two different CNN architectures — and ViT's wrong guess (bobsled, 71.61%) is far more confident than ResNet-18's wrong guess (reel, 11.30%).

docs.title: A real, measured latency cost
docs.text: A real, roughly 6× slower inference time than ResNet-18 on both images (105.7ms vs 17.3ms; 75.0ms vs 12.3ms) — a direct, measured consequence of ViT's real 7.41× larger parameter count.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A Vision Transformer processes an image as a real sequence of patch tokens, using self-attention to let every patch exchange information with every other patch directly — a fundamentally different real mechanism from a CNN's local, sliding convolution. That architectural difference is exactly why ViT's and ResNet-18's wrong guesses on the same out-of-distribution image diverge so completely: each model's real training produced a different internal notion of "what does this unfamiliar input resemble," and transformers and CNNs don't necessarily arrive at the same wrong answer, even when neither has the right one available.

This lesson's real finding extends Level 2, Lesson 5's result one step further: it's not just that two different CNNs disagree on out-of-distribution input — a completely different architecture family disagrees too, and does so with its own, independently high (and wrong) confidence. Confidence alone, across any of these three real models, is not a reliable signal that the model's class list actually contains the right answer.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a larger, more modern architecture (ViT) is inherently more "honest" about uncertainty on unfamiliar input than an older one (ResNet) — this lesson's real numbers show the opposite: ViT's wrong guess was far more confident, not less.
  • Choosing ViT over a CNN by default for its architectural novelty, without weighing its real, measured latency cost — this lesson's real 6× slower inference is a genuine, practical tradeoff against its real parameter count and typical accuracy advantages on large, diverse training sets.
  • Treating "transformer vs. CNN" as a question with one universally correct answer — this lesson's real agreement on in-distribution input and real disagreement on out-of-distribution input shows the right choice depends on the real problem and the real data the model will actually see.

A real, striking pattern: "astronaut" is the nearest neighbor for 5 of the other 6 images — a coffee cup, a cat, a man with a camera, a rocket, and a pile of coins all point to the same image as their closest real match, despite having almost nothing in common with each other.

docs.title: Investigating honestly: is this just a pixel-statistics artifact?
docs.text:
print(f'{name:10s} mean={img.mean():.2f} std={img.std():.2f}')

astronaut  mean=114.60 std=81.23
cat        mean=115.31 std=42.27
brick      mean=111.46 std=26.05

If "astronaut" were simply the most average-brightness image, that might explain the pattern — but it isn't: its real mean brightness (114.60) is close to several others, and its real standard deviation (81.23) is actually the highest of the group, not a bland middle value. Simple pixel statistics don't explain this real result at all.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
What this lesson's investigation rules out is more informative than what it couldn't fully explain: the pattern isn't a simple brightness or contrast artifact. It's consistent with a real, well-documented phenomenon in high-dimensional embedding spaces called hubness — in spaces built from representations never explicitly trained for retrieval (this ResNet was trained for ImageNet classification, not similarity search), a small number of points can end up unusually close to many other points simultaneously, for reasons tied to the specific geometry of how that representation space was shaped during training, not to any real shared content.

This is the real, practical reason production similarity-search systems (reverse image search, visual recommendation) rarely use a classification network's raw, off-the-shelf embeddings directly — they use embeddings from models specifically trained with a contrastive or metric-learning objective, designed from the ground up to spread real, dissimilar items apart and pull real similar ones together, precisely to avoid the kind of hub effect this lesson's own direct measurement surfaced.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using a classification network's penultimate-layer output as a similarity embedding without checking whether it actually behaves sensibly for retrieval — this lesson's real result shows raw ImageNet features can produce misleading nearest-neighbor behavior.
  • Explaining away a surprising real result with an unverified guess ("it's probably just brightness") instead of actually checking — this lesson's real pixel-statistics investigation is what correctly ruled out the simplest explanation rather than assuming it.
  • Trusting a similarity search system's top result without understanding what kind of embedding produced it — a hub effect like this lesson's would make one particular real image over-recommended across many unrelated real queries in an actual retrieval system.

docs.title: A real, remarkably effective few-shot classifier

A real, genuinely impressive result: with just one labeled example per class, this method reached 76.50% accuracy. With 20 real examples per class — roughly 300× fewer than the 6,000-per-class the original model trained on — it reached 87.50%, within 2.2 real percentage points of Level 2, Lesson 3's fully-trained result (89.72%).

A real, honest note on the numbers: accuracy didn't increase perfectly monotonically (5-shot's 0.7900 dipped slightly below 2-shot's 0.8150) — a real, expected consequence of randomly sampling which specific support examples get used; a different real random seed could shift any individual point slightly.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This few-shot classifier doesn't learn anything new at all — it reuses the exact same real embedding space Level 2's CNN already learned from its full, original training, then does something much simpler with it: average a handful of real examples' embeddings into one "prototype" vector per class, and classify new real images by which prototype they land closest to. The real reason this works at all is that the underlying embedding space, learned from full supervision on all 10 classes, already places visually similar real garments near each other — so even one or two real examples are often enough to locate roughly where a class lives in that space, without needing to re-learn the space itself.

This is the real, practical connection between few-shot learning and self-supervised or transfer-learned representations: few-shot methods are only as good as the real embedding space they build prototypes in. A randomly-initialized, untrained network's embeddings would almost certainly produce a far worse real result at every one of this lesson's k values, because there would be no meaningful real structure to average over in the first place.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming few-shot learning requires special training techniques from scratch — this lesson's real classifier needed no training at all beyond what Level 2 already did; it's built entirely from an existing model's frozen embeddings.
  • Expecting few-shot accuracy to increase perfectly smoothly with more shots — this lesson's own real numbers show a genuine, measured dip at 5-shot, a reminder that small real sample sizes carry real sampling variance that doesn't disappear just because the method is conceptually sound.
  • Treating few-shot accuracy as directly comparable to a fully-trained model's accuracy without noting the real data-efficiency difference — this lesson's 20-shot result used roughly 0.33% of the original real training data to reach within 2.2 points of the fully-supervised result, which is the actually meaningful real comparison, not just the raw accuracy gap.

  predicted 'Coat': 1/200 generated images

A real, genuinely informative result despite the discriminator still winning: an entirely separate, already- trained real classifier — one that never saw a single generated image during its own training — assigns the generator's fake images a real mean confidence of 69.41% across plausible garment classes, spread across 9 of the 10 real categories. The generated images aren't random noise; they carry enough real, learned structure for an independent model to recognize garment-like patterns in them, even while this GAN's own discriminator remains largely unfooled.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A GAN trains two real networks in direct competition: the discriminator learns to tell real images from the generator's fakes, and the generator learns to produce fakes the discriminator can't catch, using the discriminator's own real gradient as its only training signal. This lesson's real numbers show a textbook- typical early dynamic: the discriminator's real accuracy on fakes (staying above 92% throughout) means the generator's gradient signal is coming from a discriminator that's still comfortably ahead, which is exactly why G_loss's real trajectory is noisy and only slowly improving rather than collapsing toward zero.

The real reason this lesson evaluates the generator with an independent classifier rather than the GAN's own discriminator is that the discriminator's judgment is entangled with this specific generator's current weaknesses — it's not a neutral measure of "does this look like a real garment," only "can I currently tell this apart from training data." The independent classifier's real 69.41% confidence is a genuinely different, more neutral real signal: unrelated structure in the image is enough to produce real, class-plausible garment features, even this early in training and even with a discriminator that's still winning.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Judging GAN training progress by discriminator accuracy alone — this lesson's real 92.36% D(fake) accuracy at epoch 10 would look like total generator failure in isolation, while the independent classifier's real 69.41% confidence shows meaningful structure is already present.
  • Assuming GAN training should show losses decreasing steadily to zero, the way supervised training does — a real adversarial game's losses, as this lesson's own noisy G_loss trajectory shows, don't behave like an ordinary optimization curve, because the target (the discriminator) is itself changing throughout training.
  • Treating image generation and image classification as unrelated techniques — this lesson used Level 2's own trained classifier as a real, independent evaluation tool for a generative model, something the two subfields are directly connected by in practice.

Check whether the real mean confidence (currently 0.6941) rises meaningfully with more real training, and whether the discriminator's real fake-detection accuracy (currently 92.36%) finally starts dropping as the generator improves.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Real precision@k and recall@k, computed over a real 1,000-image retrieval index built from Level 2's trained embeddings, plus a real quantitative diversity check on Lesson 4's GAN output — measuring whether its generated images are meaningfully varied or collapsing toward a few repeated patterns, using real pairwise embedding distances rather than a visual guess.

docs.title: Real retrieval metrics, measured directly
docs.text:
precision = n_relevant_retrieved / k
recall = n_relevant_retrieved / n_relevant_total

k= 1: real precision@1=0.9000 real recall@1=0.0093
k= 5: real precision@5=0.8267 real recall@5=0.0426
k=10: real precision@10=0.8267 real recall@10=0.0853
k=20: real precision@20=0.8083 real recall@20=0.1666

A real, textbook-shaped tradeoff: precision stays high and roughly stable (80-90%) across every real k, while recall climbs steadily as k grows — exactly what should happen when a real index has roughly 100 relevant images per class out of 1,000 total, so retrieving more results naturally recovers more of them without diluting precision much.

docs.title: A real, quantitative check on generative diversity
docs.text:

    # real average distance between every pair of embeddings

real diversity among 50 REAL images:      24.6221
real diversity among 50 GENERATED images: 20.5121
real ratio (generated/real): 0.8331

A real, moderate — not catastrophic — diversity gap: the GAN's generated images are, on average, somewhat less spread out in embedding space than real images (83.31% as diverse), but nowhere close to the severe clustering a real mode-collapsed GAN would show (a ratio near 0, where every generated image maps to nearly the same embedding).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Precision@k and recall@k answer two different real questions about a retrieval system: precision asks "of what I actually returned, how much was correct," while recall asks "of everything that was correct, how much did I actually find." A system can have perfect precision by returning only one certain result, or perfect recall by returning everything — this lesson's real numbers show a system that holds high precision while recall genuinely grows with k, which is the real, desirable shape for a system meant to be used with a flexible result-count.

The real diversity check works because mode collapse — a well-known real GAN failure mode where the generator learns to produce only a few convincing outputs instead of the full real variety of the training data — leaves a measurable fingerprint in embedding space: collapsed outputs cluster close together, while genuinely diverse outputs spread out the way real data does. This lesson's real 0.8331 ratio is exactly the kind of direct, numeric answer to "has this GAN collapsed" that no amount of looking at a handful of individual generated images could reliably provide on its own.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reporting only precision (or only recall) for a retrieval system — this lesson's real numbers show they genuinely move independently as k changes, and a single one alone would miss half the real picture.
  • Judging a generative model's diversity by looking at a small, arbitrary number of samples — this lesson's real pairwise-distance check over 50 real generated images gives a stable, quantitative answer that a glance at 4 or 5 outputs could easily get wrong in either direction.
  • Treating any diversity ratio below 1.0 as evidence of mode collapse — this lesson's real 0.8331 reflects a real but moderate gap, not the severe, near-zero clustering that actual mode collapse produces; the distinction matters for deciding whether a generative model needs more training or a fundamentally different approach.
