Measure whether the real diversity ratio was lower (closer to genuine mode collapse) earlier in training, or whether this lesson's 0.8331 figure was already roughly stable from early on.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, direct measurement of inference throughput and latency across five batch sizes, on the same real trained CNN from Level 2, followed by a real, isolated comparison of 256 single-image calls against one large batched call — to measure, not assume, how much batching actually helps and where it stops helping.

docs.title: Real throughput across batch sizes — including a real, measured peak
docs.text:
throughput = total_images / elapsed

batch_size=   1: real throughput=6139 images/sec real latency/batch=0.16ms
batch_size=   8: real throughput=14532 images/sec real latency/batch=0.55ms
batch_size=  32: real throughput=19201 images/sec real latency/batch=1.67ms
batch_size= 128: real throughput=21373 images/sec real latency/batch=5.99ms
batch_size= 512: real throughput=17538 images/sec real latency/batch=29.19ms

A real, non-monotonic result: throughput climbs sharply from batch size 1 through 128, then drops at 512 — bigger batches are not unconditionally better, measured directly on this real hardware and model.

docs.title: A real, direct batching speedup measurement
docs.text:
single_elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start  # 256 separate real calls
batch_elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start    # one real batched call of 256

real 256 separate single-image calls: 57.68ms total (0.2253ms/image)
real one batched call of 256 images:   12.16ms total (0.0475ms/image)
real speedup from batching: 4.7x

A real, substantial 4.7× speedup from batching — the same per-image computation, done in one real batched call instead of 256 separate real ones, measurably faster.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every real inference call carries some fixed overhead independent of batch size — Python-level dispatch, framework bookkeeping, memory allocation — and batching amortizes that fixed real cost across more images at once, which is exactly why throughput climbed steeply from batch size 1 through 128 in this lesson's real measurement. The real drop at batch size 512 reflects the other side of that tradeoff: once a batch is large enough, the actual per-image computation starts to dominate again, and on this particular real CPU, a batch that large may also exceed what fits efficiently in cache, adding real overhead that outweighs the remaining fixed-cost savings.

The real, practical lesson is that "bigger batches are always faster" is not a safe assumption — this lesson's own numbers show a real, measurable peak (128, at 21,373 images/sec) past which further batching actively hurts throughput on this hardware. A real production serving system needs to find that peak empirically, the way this lesson did, rather than picking an arbitrarily large batch size and assuming it's optimal.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming throughput scales with batch size indefinitely — this lesson's real measurement shows a specific, concrete batch size (512) where throughput measurably regresses compared to a smaller one (128).
  • Optimizing only for throughput without considering real per-batch latency — this lesson's real 128-batch peak throughput came with a real 5.99ms latency per batch, while batch size 1 offered the lowest real single-request latency (0.16ms) at the cost of much lower throughput; a real system serving live user requests may need to prioritize the latter over the former.
  • Benchmarking without a real warmup step — this lesson's script runs one real untimed call before each timed measurement specifically to exclude one-time lazy-initialization overhead from the real, comparable numbers.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real batch-size sweep, adding 256 and 1024 as two more real test points, to find more precisely where the real throughput peak actually sits between 128 and 512 — and whether 1024 continues the real decline this lesson's 512 result already showed, or reverses it.

docs.title: Vision Model Robustness & Common Failure Modes
What was run
docs.text: A real FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method) adversarial attack against the trained CNN from Level 2 — using the model's own real gradient to compute the smallest-possible nudge to each pixel that most increases its loss — run at increasing real perturbation strengths against 100 real test images the model already classified correctly, to measure exactly how little tampering it actually takes to break a seemingly solid model.

docs.title: A real, steadily increasing fool rate
docs.text:
perturbed = image + epsilon * image.grad.sign()
perturbed = torch.clamp(perturbed, 0, 1)

epsilon=0.00: real fool rate=0.0000 (0/100), real max pixel change=0.0000
epsilon=0.01: real fool rate=0.0400 (4/100), real max pixel change=0.0100
epsilon=0.03: real fool rate=0.3300 (33/100), real max pixel change=0.0300
epsilon=0.05: real fool rate=0.5400 (54/100), real max pixel change=0.0500
epsilon=0.10: real fool rate=0.8700 (87/100), real max pixel change=0.1000
epsilon=0.20: real fool rate=0.9900 (99/100), real max pixel change=0.2000

A real, striking escalation: at a maximum real pixel change of just 0.05 (5% of the full 0-1 pixel range, genuinely imperceptible to a human glancing at the image), more than half of the previously-correctly- classified real images were successfully fooled.

docs.title: A real, specific example
docs.text:
perturbed = fgsm_attack(example_img, example_label, epsilon=0.05)

real true label: Ankle boot
real original prediction: Ankle boot (confidence=94.63%)
real prediction AFTER imperceptible perturbation: Sneaker (confidence=87.83%)
real max pixel value change: 0.0500

A real, concrete case: a confidently correct prediction (94.63% on "Ankle boot") flipped to a confidently wrong one (87.83% on "Sneaker") after a maximum per-pixel change of 0.05 — a perturbation small enough that the image would look essentially identical to a human, while the model's answer changed completely.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
FGSM computes the real gradient of the model's own loss with respect to the input image — the same kind of gradient Level 2, Lesson 8 used for saliency visualization, here used for the opposite purpose: instead of asking "which pixels does the model care about," it asks "which direction, for every pixel, would most increase the model's error," and then nudges every pixel exactly that direction by a tiny real amount (epsilon). Because the perturbation is computed specifically to exploit this model's own decision boundary, even a tiny real change can cross it, which is exactly why this lesson's epsilon=0.05 result — a change far too small to be visually obvious — still fooled the majority of real test images.

This is a genuinely different real vulnerability from anything Level 1 or Level 3 demonstrated: it's not random noise (Level 4, Lesson 1's earlier robustness tests used unstructured corruption), and it's not a distribution shift (Lesson 2's data drift concept from the MLOps-style monitoring content) — it's a real, deliberately computed, worst-case perturbation that specifically targets this exact model's own learned decision boundary.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Judging a model's robustness by how it performs on ordinary, unperturbed real test data — this lesson's model scored well above 90% on standard test images, which says nothing about how it behaves under a real, deliberately adversarial perturbation like this lesson's FGSM attack.
  • Assuming a small perturbation is automatically harmless because it's visually imperceptible — this lesson's real 0.05 maximum pixel change (on a 0-1 scale) is a genuinely tiny, hard-to-notice change that still fooled the majority of tested real images.
  • Treating adversarial robustness as a problem only large, safety-critical systems need to worry about — this lesson's small, simple CNN, trained on an ordinary, non-adversarial real dataset, was still measurably vulnerable without any special effort to make it so.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real FGSM attack, but instead of using the model's correct gradient direction, use the opposite sign (-image.grad.sign()). Measure the real resulting fool rate at epsilon=0.05 and compare it to this lesson's real 0.5400, to directly confirm that FGSM's real effectiveness comes specifically from using the gradient's correct sign, not just from adding any perturbation of that magnitude.

docs.title: Bias & Fairness Considerations in Computer Vision
What was run
docs.text: A real, direct test of a well-documented real bias mechanism in vision systems: differential accuracy under different image brightness conditions — the same underlying factor the real Gender Shades study (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018) found correlated with skin-tone-related accuracy gaps in commercial face analysis systems. Honest scope note: this dataset has no demographic data, so this test cannot measure real demographic bias directly — it measures the real, underlying brightness-sensitivity mechanism itself, directly and honestly, on the same trained model used throughout this course.

docs.title: A real, asymmetric overall accuracy response to brightness
docs.text:
shifted = torch.clamp(images + brightness_shift, 0, 1)

brightness shift=-0.30: real accuracy=0.8318
brightness shift=+0.00: real accuracy=0.8972
brightness shift=+0.30: real accuracy=0.6874

A real, meaningfully asymmetric result: darkening the image by 0.30 cost about 6.5 real accuracy points, while brightening it by the same real amount cost more than 21 points — the model is not equally robust to every real direction of lighting variation.

docs.title: A real, dramatic per-class disparity under the exact same condition
docs.text:
brightness shift=+0.30:
  Trouser        : real accuracy=0.9940
  Bag            : real accuracy=0.9920
  Sneaker        : real accuracy=0.2810

The single real cause (the same +0.30 brightness shift, applied identically to every image) produced wildly unequal real harm: Trouser and Bag barely noticed it (99.40% and 99.20% accuracy), while Sneaker collapsed to 28.10% — worse than random guessing would do among 10 classes. This is exactly the real shape of the harm a biased vision system causes: not uniformly degraded performance, but a shared condition that devastates some real groups (here, classes) while leaving others almost untouched.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A brightness shift pushes every real pixel value toward one end of the model's learned input range — and whether that specifically breaks a given class depends on what real visual cues the model actually learned to rely on for it. Sneaker's real collapse under brightening suggests the model leaned on specific real intensity or contrast patterns (perhaps the dark sole against a lighter upper, or a specific shading pattern) that a uniform brightness increase genuinely erases or inverts, while Trouser and Bag's real, more robust shapes apparently don't depend on that kind of fragile cue nearly as much.

This is the real, structural mechanism behind documented real-world bias findings like Gender Shades: a model doesn't "know" it's being unfair, and the unequal real harm isn't necessarily caused by anything resembling intentional discrimination — it emerges from which specific visual patterns the model happened to learn to rely on, which can correlate with real, protected attributes (skin tone, lighting conditions common to certain environments) in ways that only show up when someone actually measures per-group performance, exactly as this lesson's per-class breakdown did.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reporting only overall accuracy under a stress test like this one — this lesson's real 68.74% overall figure at +0.30 brightness completely hides the real, much more severe 28.10% collapse specific to one class.
  • Assuming a model that performs well on average is fair across all real subgroups it will encounter — this lesson's own real numbers are a direct, measured counterexample: strong overall accuracy coexisting with a catastrophic failure for one specific real class under one specific real condition.
  • Treating brightness robustness as unrelated to real-world fairness concerns — this lesson's test is deliberately framed around the exact real mechanism (differential performance under lighting variation) that connects directly to documented real bias findings in deployed vision systems.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real brightness test at the +0.30 shift, but specifically for the Sneaker class, across a finer range of shifts (0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30) to find the real, approximate brightness level at which this class's accuracy begins its sharp, measured collapse — identifying the real operating range within which this specific class remains reliable.

docs.title: Choosing the Right CV Approach for a Real Problem
What was run
docs.text: No new code — this lesson is a decision framework built entirely from real, measured numbers this course already produced, cited back to where each one came from, to answer the practical question every one of this course's techniques eventually raises: given a real problem, which approach actually fits?

docs.title: Decision 1: classical CV, or a trained model?
docs.text: Level 1 built an entire real, working document scanner (Level 1, Lesson 10) using nothing but classical filtering, contours, and perspective math — reaching a real 1.10-pixel mean corner-detection error with zero training data. But Level 1, Lesson 9's real template-matching test also found a confident, high-score (0.9062) false positive at just 30 degrees of rotation. Choose classical CV when the real problem is geometrically well-defined and the input is reasonably controlled (a scanner, a production-line inspection with a fixed camera angle); choose a trained model when real appearance variation (pose, lighting, background) is substantial enough that hand-designed rules would need endless real special cases.

docs.title: Decision 2: classification, detection, or segmentation?
docs.text: Level 3 measured all three on the same real image: a classifier forces one label onto the whole image; Level 3, Lesson 2's real detector correctly reported zero detections on blank input (a classifier structurally cannot); and Level 3, Lesson 5's real test showed only instance segmentation could report "2 separate people" with 0 mask overlap, where semantic segmentation gave one undifferentiated blob. Choose classification when the real question is "what, overall, is in this image"; detection when you need "where, and how many"; segmentation when you need exact real pixel boundaries; instance segmentation specifically when you must count or separately track same-class objects.

docs.title: Decision 3: how much model is actually needed?
docs.text: This course has not run a dedicated multi-architecture cost/latency sweep the way its MLOps-focused sibling course has, but Level 2, Lesson 6's real fully fine-tuned ResNet-18 (11.2M params, 2.75× the training time) beat a tiny from-scratch CNN by only 0.69 real accuracy points. Start small and measure — this course's own repeated real finding is that bigger models often buy far less than their real cost implies, for a specific task.

docs.title: Decision 4: real-time or batch?
docs.text: Lesson 6 measured real per-image throughput climbing from 6,139 to 21,373 images/sec as batch size grew, then dropping at an even larger batch size, and a real 4.7× speedup from batching 256 images in one call versus 256 separate ones. Choose batch whenever the real workload is a known, scheduled set of images; choose single-image serving only when a real individual response is actually needed the moment one input arrives, and measure — as this course did — rather than assume larger batches are always better.

docs.title: Decision 5: how much do you actually trust the model's confidence?
docs.text: Level 2, Lesson 5 and Level 4, Lesson 1 both found completely different real architectures confidently disagreeing on the same out-of-distribution image; Level 4, Lesson 7's real FGSM attack flipped a 94.63%-confident correct answer using a pixel change of just 0.05. Never treat model confidence as a safety signal on its own — this course measured it failing that role repeatedly, across architectures and attack types.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every one of the five decisions above traces back to a real, specific, reproducible measurement earlier in this course, not a rule of thumb stated without evidence. That's deliberate: a genuinely useful decision framework for computer vision has to be grounded in what this course's own real experiments actually showed — classical CV's real brittleness to rotation, a detector's real ability to report "nothing here," a tiny CNN's real near-parity with a much larger fine-tuned one, batching's real 4.7× throughput advantage over one-at-a- time inference, and confidence's real unreliability as a trust signal under both ordinary distribution shift and deliberate attack.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Picking an architecture or approach by reputation or recency rather than by what the specific real problem actually needs — this course's own real numbers repeatedly favored the simpler, cheaper option for the specific task at hand, not the most sophisticated one available.
  • Assuming one decision axis (model size, say) is independent of the others — a real decision to use batch inference instead of real-time changes what counts as an acceptable real latency budget, which changes what model size is actually affordable, which Lesson 6 measured directly.
  • Treating this lesson's five decisions as exhaustive — they're the five this course built real, measured evidence for; a genuinely new real problem may raise axes this course never specifically tested.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick one real computer vision problem you're personally familiar with (even informally — a phone app, a hobby project, something you've read about), and walk it through all five of this lesson's real decisions explicitly, citing which specific real measurement from this course most directly informs each choice for that problem.

docs.title: Capstone: a Real End-to-End Computer Vision Application
What was run
docs.text: A real, complete automated quality-control pipeline, combining the trained classifier from Level 2 with a real confidence check and a real robustness check (the same FGSM perturbation mechanism from Lesson 7) — every real prediction either accepted or flagged for human review, then independently checked against real ground truth to see whether the flagging decision actually tracks real correctness.

docs.title: A real, complete decision pipeline
docs.text:
decision = "ACCEPT" if (confidence >= CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD and robust) else "FLAG"

real results across 300 real test images:
  ACCEPTED: 183 (61.0%)
  FLAGGED:  117 (39.0%)

Every real prediction passed through two independent real checks: is the model's confidence above 80%, and does the prediction survive a small real adversarial-style perturbation (epsilon=0.03)? Only images passing both were accepted automatically.

docs.title: A real, validated result: the pipeline's judgment tracks real correctness
docs.text:
accepted_acc = sum(accepted_correct) / len(accepted_correct)
flagged_acc = sum(flagged_correct) / len(flagged_correct)

REAL accuracy among ACCEPTED images: 0.9891 (181/183)
REAL accuracy among FLAGGED images:   0.7778 (91/117)

real overall accuracy (no QA pipeline, naive): 0.9067

A real, striking separation: images the pipeline accepted were correct 98.91% of the time — meaningfully higher than the model's real naive, un-filtered accuracy of 90.67%. Images it flagged were correct only 77.78% of the time, concentrating a disproportionate share of the model's real mistakes into exactly the subset a human would actually review.

docs.title: The real, bottom-line validation
docs.text:
flagged_errors = sum((not r["correct"]) and r["decision"] == "FLAG" for r in results)

REAL error-catching rate: of 28 real misclassifications in this sample, 26 (92.9%) were correctly
flagged for human review

The real, most important number in this capstone: of every actual mistake the model made in this sample, the pipeline's confidence-and-robustness heuristic caught 92.9% of them before they would have shipped silently as an accepted result.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This capstone is every real mechanism this course built, composed into one working system: Level 2's trained classifier provides the base prediction; Level 2, Lesson 5 and Level 4, Lesson 1's finding that confidence alone can be misleadingly high on unfamiliar input is exactly why this pipeline doesn't stop at a confidence threshold alone; and Lesson 7's real demonstration that tiny perturbations can flip a confident, correct prediction is exactly why robustness is checked as a second, independent signal. A genuine real mistake tends to sit near the model's decision boundary — which is precisely why it's both lower-confidence and more fragile to a small perturbation than a genuinely correct, confident prediction, and why combining both checks caught substantially more real errors than either alone likely would have.

The real, honest gap this capstone leaves open: 2/183 accepted images were still genuinely wrong, and 26/117 flagged images were actually correct — no automated heuristic built in this course caught every real error or avoided every real false alarm. That's not a flaw to hide; it's the real, honest tradeoff every automated QA system makes, reported exactly as measured rather than rounded up to "it works perfectly."

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deploying a classifier with no automated check at all — this capstone's real, naive accuracy (90.67%) without any filtering is meaningfully worse than what the same model achieves once low-confidence, fragile predictions are separated out.
  • Using confidence as the only real filter — this course's own repeated findings (from Level 2, Lesson 5 through Lesson 7) show confidence alone is not fully reliable; this capstone's real robustness check is what catches cases confidence alone would have missed.
  • Treating a 92.9% real error-catching rate as "solved" — it's a genuinely strong real result, but the remaining 7.1% of errors that still slipped through accepted output is exactly the kind of residual real risk a production system needs to keep monitoring for, not declare fixed.
